verdict.summary:
MEMORANDUM — STATUS OF THE FRCP APPENDIX OF FORMS AND THE EFFECTIVE DATE OF ITS CHANGE

I. SHORT ANSWER

1. Status (ask 1): ABROGATED. In the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended to December 1, 2025, there is no operative Appendix of Forms. Title XII, "APPENDIX OF FORMS," appears only as a stub reading "[Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" The enabling rule, Rule 84 ("Forms"), was abrogated in the same package and appears as "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015."

2. Effective date (ask 2): DECEMBER 1, 2015. The change was made by the Supreme Court's order of April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 2072, and took effect on December 1, 2015. April 29, 2015 is the order/transmittal date, not the effective date; do not use it as the operative date.

3. The December 1, 2025 amendments did not touch this. The abrogation predates them by ten years and remains in force; the current text "as amended to December 1, 2025" still shows Title XII as abrogated.

II. AUTHORITY RELIED ON

A. Supreme Court order, April 29, 2015 (supremecourt.gov, "frcv15(update)_1823.pdf").
   - "ORDERED: 1. That the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure be, and they hereby are, amended by including therein amendments to Civil Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, 55, and 84, and the Appendix of Forms."
   - "2. That the foregoing amendments to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure shall take effect on December 1, 2015, and shall govern in all proceedings in civil cases thereafter commenced and, insofar as just and practicable, all proceedings then pending."
   - Transmitted text: "Rule 84. Forms [Abrogated (Apr. __, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and "APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. __, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" (The blank day in the transmitted text is the placeholder in the proposed amendments; the order itself is dated April 29, 2015.)

B. Federal Judicial Center, amendments page for Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (fjc.gov).
   - "Amendments to the following Federal Rules of Civil Procedure became effective on December 1, 2015: 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated."
   - Companion entry: "Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Transmittal to Congress, April 29, 2015."

C. Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure index (law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp), expressly "as amended to December 1, 2025."
   - "Rule 84. Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015"
   - "XII. APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"

Source caveat: the uscourts.gov FRCP landing page does not itself mention the Appendix of Forms and does not contain the string "December 1, 2025"; it says only that "[t]he Civil Rules were last amended in 2025" and links the "Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Pamphlet, Dec. 1, 2025." The answer therefore rests on the three sources above (A–C), not on that landing page.

III. CHRONOLOGY (each date labeled by its role)

- April 29, 2015 — date of the Supreme Court order amending Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, 55, and 84 and the Appendix of Forms; transmitted to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 2072.
- December 1, 2015 — EFFECTIVE DATE of those amendments, including the abrogation of Rule 84 and of the Appendix of Forms. This is the date the change took effect.
- December 1, 2025 — date through which the current rules text is amended; the Appendix of Forms remains abrogated as of that date. No 2025 amendment revived, replaced, or renumbered it.

IV. WHAT THE STATUS IS NOT (negative findings, to prevent miscitation)

- Not "superseded" or "renumbered." Abrogation removed Title XII and Rule 84 outright; there is no successor appendix and no new rule number to which the old forms were moved.
- Not a 2025 change. Nothing in the 2025 amendment cycle is the source; a manual updated to 2025 must still record the 2015 abrogation.
- Not a statutory repeal by Congress. The change came through the Rules Enabling Act process (Supreme Court order, transmitted to Congress, effective absent contrary congressional action).
- Not to be confused with other form sets. The Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure forms, the Bankruptcy Official Forms, and the court's AO forms are separate instruments and were not affected by this abrogation.

V. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE 2014 MANUAL (practice consequences)

The manual's direction to "see the Appendix of Forms" is now a dead reference. Consequences to build into the update:

1. Every citation of the form "Fed. R. Civ. P. Form __" (e.g., Form 11, Form 18, Form 52) is obsolete as a rule citation. Form 18 (complaint for negligence) in particular should not be cited as supplying a pleading standard; the model-form safe harbor it represented is gone.
2. The substantive content did not vanish from practice — it migrated to the Administrative Office forms and to the rules themselves. Practical substitutes practitioners now use (confirm each against uscourts.gov before relying on it in the manual):
   - Summons — AO 440.
   - Waiver of the Service of Summons — AO 398; Notice of a Lawsuit and Request to Waive Service — AO 399.
   - Civil Cover Sheet — JS 44.
   - Subpoena — AO 88A / AO 88B.
   - Judgment — AO 450.
   These are court forms, not rule text; cite them as AO/JS forms, not as FRCP forms.
3. Local practice: many districts maintain their own forms and local rules on service, default judgment, and scheduling. The manual should add a step telling users to check the district's local rules and website, because after abrogation there is no single national form set in the FRCP to fall back on.
4. Broader review: a 2014 manual is now at least eleven years stale. Beyond this one reference, audit for (a) the 2015 amendments to Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55 (including the discovery proportionality and preservation changes), (b) later amendment cycles through December 1, 2025, and (c) any reliance on model forms as statements of governing law.

VI. REPLACEMENT DRAFTING LANGUAGE FOR THE MANUAL

Delete: "See the Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure for the applicable form."

Substitute: "The Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure was abrogated effective December 1, 2015 (Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015; Rule 84 abrogated in the same order). There are no longer official forms appended to the Civil Rules. For national forms, use the Administrative Office forms available at uscourts.gov (e.g., AO 440 Summons; AO 398/399 waiver of service; JS 44 Civil Cover Sheet). Check the local rules and the district court's website for any district-specific form requirements."

VII. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR THE REVIEWER

1. Open the current FRCP text as amended to December 1, 2025 and confirm Title XII reads "APPENDIX OF FORMS [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]" and Rule 84 reads "Abrogated, eff. Dec. 1, 2015."
2. Confirm the effective date, December 1, 2015, in the Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015 (paragraph 2 of the ORDERED clauses), not from the order's date line.
3. Confirm that the December 1, 2025 pamphlet carries the abrogation forward unchanged.
4. Confirm no local rule in the relevant district re-adopts FRCP form numbering.

VIII. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE TWO ASKS

- Ask 1 — status: abrogated (Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms, abrogated by the Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015).
- Ask 2 — effective date of the change: December 1, 2015.

The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure govern civil proceedings in the United States district courts.

The purpose of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure is "to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action and proceeding." Fed. R. Civ. P. 1. The rules were first adopted by order of the Supreme Court on December 20, 1937, transmitted to Congress on January 3, 1938, and effective September 16, 1938. The Civil Rules were last amended in 2025.

Protocol No. 14
Protocol No. 14 amending the Convention introduced a new admissibility criterion, the treatment of repetitive cases or clearly inadmissible cases, for a more satisfactory operation of the Court.
Under the Protocol the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe is empowered, if it decides by a two-thirds majority to do so, to bring proceedings before the Court where a State refuses to comply with a judgment. The Committee of Ministers is also empowered to ask the Court for an interpretation of a judgment. This is to assist the Committee of Ministers in its task of supervising the execution of judgments and particularly in determining what measures may be necessary to comply with a judgment.
Other measures in the Protocol include changing the judges' term of office to a single, nine year term, and a provision allowing the accession by the European Union to the Convention.

verdict.summary:
CORRECTION MEMORANDUM — TRAINING SLIDE: ECtHR JUDGES' TERMS OF OFFICE
Prepared: 22 November 2026 | Governing text: ECHR as amended by Protocols No. 14 and No. 15 (English version)

1. BOTTOM LINE
1.1 The election term is NINE YEARS (9).
1.2 A judge MAY NOT be re-elected. The term is a single, non-renewable term.
1.3 The slide's statement ('renewable six-year terms') is WRONG as a statement of current law. It describes the regime that ceased to apply to judges elected from 1 June 2010 onwards. The error originates in Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94), not in Protocol No. 15 — Protocol No. 15 did not alter the length or the renewability of the term at all.

2. CONTROLLING PROVISION AND EXACT WORDING
2.1 Provision: Article 23 (Terms of office and dismissal), paragraph 1, of the Convention as amended.
2.2 Verbatim (numbered-article format, ETS 5 consolidated text, https://rm.coe.int/1680a2353d, sha256 ba0fe36805b8):
    "Article 23 – Terms of office and dismissal
     1  The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
     2  The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration."
2.3 Verbatim (ECHR official text presented as amended by Protocol No. 15, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG, sha256 cc3ebf842b81):
    "ARTICLE 23 — Terms of office and dismissal
     1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
     2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration."
2.4 Third, corroborating official quotation (PACE/Secretary General guidance on the election procedure, SG-AS (2026) 01, https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf, sha256 449564d229b2, para. 13): "Article 23 of the Convention, as amended by Protocol No. 15 to the Convention, stipulates: '1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected. 2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.'"
2.5 Election mechanism (context, unchanged): Article 22 — judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly, in respect of each High Contracting Party, by a majority of votes cast, from a list of three candidates nominated by that Party. Article 23 §1 fixes the term; Article 22 fixes the manner of election. The two must be cited together in any corrected slide.

3. ANSWERS TO THE TWO QUESTIONS ASKED
3.1 'What is the election term?' — Nine years. Article 23 §1, first sentence. (Results entry: ask 1 = 9 years.)
3.2 'May a judge be re-elected?' — No. Article 23 §1, second sentence: 'They may not be re-elected.' Note for accuracy in the slide: Article 25 §1(a) and (c) do allow re-election, but only of the President/Vice-Presidents and of Chamber Presidents in their institutional capacities — not of judges to the Court. Do not let that coincidence of wording be misread as permitting a judge's re-election; it concerns internal office-holders, not the judicial mandate.

4. WHY THE SLIDE IS WRONG (DIAGNOSIS, FOR THE TRAINER'S NOTE)
4.1 Pre-1 June 2010 regime: judges were elected for a renewable six-year term. That is the source of the slide's wording.
4.2 Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) replaced this with a single nine-year term. The ECHR 'Protocols' page states that the measures in Protocol No. 14 include 'changing the judges' term of office to a single, nine year term' (https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols, sha256 35fce35b4cec). Protocol No. 14 entered into force on 1 June 2010 — recited on the face of the amended Convention: 'The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010.'
4.3 Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), in force 1 August 2021, did NOT change Article 23 §1's term or the bar on re-election. Its effects on judges' terms were indirect:
    (a) it deleted the former Article 23 §2, which had provided that a judge's term expired on reaching the age of 70 (SG-AS (2026) 01, footnote 26: 'Former paragraph 2 of Article 23 ("The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70") was deleted by Protocol 15');
    (b) it inserted a new Article 21 §2: 'Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.'
    The Protocol No. 15 explanatory report confirms the linkage: the change was intended 'to enable highly qualified judges to serve the full nine-year term of office', and the age limit was 'no longer essential ... given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable' (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng, sha256 d85a250bb703, paras 11–12). Note the premise: nine years, non-renewable — i.e. the Protocol 14 rule is treated as settled background by Protocol 15.
4.4 Conclusion for the slide: the error is a regime-confusion error of roughly sixteen years' standing, not a Protocol 15 point. Any trainer's note should say so explicitly, because a reviewer who checks only Protocol 15 will find nothing in it about six years and may wrongly conclude the slide is fine.

5. TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS — CAVEAT TO STATE, NOT TO OVERSTATE
5.1 Transitional rules can make old-law statements true of individual judges without being true of the Convention text. Protocol No. 15's own transitional provision (Article 8 §1) applies the Article 21 §2 age criterion only to judges elected from lists submitted after entry into force; judges on previously submitted lists, including judges in office and judges-elect at 1 August 2021, remain subject to the pre-existing rule (expiry at 70) — explanatory report, para. 15.
5.2 Protocol No. 14 likewise carried transitional arrangements for judges elected before its entry into force. I have NOT re-verified the verbatim text of Protocol No. 14's transitional article in this exercise and therefore do not quote or paraphrase it. If the training audience includes judges elected before 1 June 2010, obtain the text of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94) and its explanatory report before asserting which individual mandates ran on the six-year renewable basis.
5.3 The safe formulation for the slide: 'Judges are elected for a single, non-renewable nine-year term (Article 23 §1). Mandates begun under the pre-1 June 2010 six-year renewable regime continued under the rules applicable at the time of election.'

6. DROP-IN REPLACEMENT TEXT FOR THE SLIDE
6.1 Headline (replaces 'renewable six-year terms'):
    "Judges of the European Court of Human Rights are elected for a single term of nine years. They may not be re-elected."
6.2 Citation line (place under the headline, small type):
    "ECHR, Article 23 §1, as amended by Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 94, in force 1 June 2010) and presented as amended by Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021)."
6.3 Optional supporting bullet: "Judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly from a list of three candidates nominated by the State concerned (Article 22). They hold office until replaced and continue to deal with cases already under consideration (Article 23 §2). Candidates must be under 65 at the date the list of three is requested (Article 21 §2, inserted by Protocol No. 15)."
6.4 Historical footnote, if the deck keeps an 'evolution' panel: "Until 1 June 2010 judges served renewable six-year terms; Protocol No. 14 replaced this with a single nine-year term."

7. EVIDENCE TABLE (what each source establishes)
7.1 https://rm.coe.int/1680a2353d (ETS 5 consolidated, sha256 ba0fe36805b8, fetched 2026-11-22): Article 23 §1 text; Article 22; Article 21; footnote recording that the Article 21/23 amendments take effect under Protocol No. 15 from 1 August 2021.
7.2 https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG (sha256 cc3ebf842b81, fetched 2026-11-22): same Article 23 §1 text; express statement that the text is presented as amended by Protocols No. 15 (from 1 August 2021) and No. 14 (from 1 June 2010); 'Entry into force: 01/08/2021'.
7.3 https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf (SG-AS (2026) 01, sha256 449564d229b2, fetched 2026-11-22): quotes Article 23 §§1–2 as amended by Protocol No. 15; confirms deletion of the former Article 23 §2 age-70 rule; describes commencement of the nine-year term.
7.4 https://www.echr.coe.int/protocols (sha256 35fce35b4cec, fetched 2026-11-22): Protocol No. 14 'changing the judges' term of office to a single, nine year term' — the bridge between the slide's six-year claim and the current text.
7.5 https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng (sha256 d85a250bb703, fetched 2026-11-22): paras 11–15 — purpose of the new Article 21 §2, deletion of the age limit, and the transitional rule in Article 8 §1.

8. DISCLOSURE: PROOF OF ABSENCE ON ONE PAGE, AND WHY IT DOES NOT CONTROL
8.1 The harness holds a proof of absence for ask 1 in respect of https://search.coe.int/cm/eng?i=091259488028055b (1,750 characters, sha256 158056c349fc): none of 'term', 'mandate', 'duration', 'period', 'six years', '6 yr', '6-year term' appears anywhere in its full text.
8.2 That finding is correct and irrelevant to the answer: the page is a Committee of Ministers search/landing page, not a text of the Convention. It states nothing about judges' terms, and nothing in this memorandum relies on it. Because the ask is answered — expressly, and in three independent official sources — this is not a case in which 'the page states none' is the answer to the question, so ask 1 is not recorded as not stated.
8.3 Conversely, no part of the answer rests on inference from silence. Article 23 §1 states both the term and the bar on re-election in terms.

9. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS ADVICE
9.1 The English version is treated as controlling (per the project assumption). Other language versions were not compared; a divergence check is unnecessary for a training slide in English but should be run before the wording is used in any multilingual or legally operative document.
9.2 Article 23 §1 as quoted is the Convention text; the Court's internal organisation (Presidents, Registrar, Chamber Presidents, Article 25) is expressly outside this answer except for the warning at 3.2.
9.3 Edge case flagged, not resolved: the position of a judge who leaves office before completing a nine-year term and is later proposed again. 'They may not be re-elected' bars re-election to the Court; whether a fresh election after an incomplete mandate is legally possible is a question on which specific advice should be taken from the Registry/PACE Secretariat before it is asserted in training material. It does not affect the two answers given.
9.4 If the deck also states the application time-limit or other Protocol No. 15 changes, note for the reviewer that Protocol No. 15 reduced the time-limit from six to four months (ECHR 'Protocols' page). That 'six' is a different six from the slide's term error and must not be conflated when the deck is corrected.

10. VERDICT
10.1 Ask 1: election term = 9 years. Re-election: not permitted (Article 23 §1, ECHR as amended through Protocol No. 15).
10.2 The slide must be corrected, not merely annotated: replace 'renewable six-year terms' with 'a single, non-renewable nine-year term', cite Article 23 §1, and — if the historical regime is retained for teaching purposes — label it expressly as pre-1 June 2010 law superseded by Protocol No. 14.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER
1. No. A State-aid team cannot rely on Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (GBER) to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from the Article 108(3) TFEU notification obligation. That category is expressly excluded from the GBER's scope.

2. The instrument identified by the GBER's scope passage is Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24). The Regulation cites it as 'Council Decision No 2010/787' in Article 1(3)(d) and as 'Council Decision 2010/787/EU' in the consolidated text.

TEXTUAL BASIS
- GBER Article 1(3) provides: 'This Regulation shall not apply to: ... (d) aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787'. The same exclusion appears in the original and consolidated versions; the consolidated 2020 text reads 'as covered by Council Decision 2010/787/EU'.
- GBER Recital 12 states: 'This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'
- GBER Article 2(13) defines 'coal' by reference to the same Council decision of 10 December 2010, confirming that the closure-aid category is governed by that instrument rather than by the GBER.

LEGAL EFFECT
- The GBER is a block-exemption instrument: aid must fall within its material and personal scope before any exemption from notification can operate. Because Article 1(3)(d) places closure aid for uncompetitive coal mines outside the GBER's scope, no GBER article can supply the exemption. The notification duty in Article 108(3) TFEU therefore remains unless another applicable instrument covers the measure.
- The exclusion is category-specific. It is not a blanket exclusion of all coal-sector aid: Recital 12 states that the GBER should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, except regional aid. The carve-out is for aid 'to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'.
- The identified instrument is Council Decision 2010/787/EU. Whether a particular measure can be granted without individual notification, and on what conditions, must be assessed under that Decision and its own procedural and temporal provisions, not under the GBER. The Decision is time-limited (it applied until 31 December 2018 under its own terms, subject to its provisions); its temporal validity must be checked for the grant date in question. If the Decision no longer applies, the GBER carve-out still prevents reliance on the GBER, and the measure would need to be assessed directly against the Treaty and notification rules.

ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE
- I do not enter ask 2 in not_stated. The harness's proof of absence searched for strings such as 'Coal Mine Closure Aid (CMCA)', 'Coal Mine Closure Instrument (CMCI)', 'Coal Mine Closure Scheme', etc. Those are not the designation used by Regulation 651/2014. The fetched page expressly contains 'Council Decision No 2010/787' in Article 1(3)(d), and the recital on the same page names the 'Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'. The answer is therefore stated in the grounding, not absent from it.

RESULT VALUES
- Ask 1: No (verdict).
- Ask 2: Council Decision 2010/787/EU (identifier).

State funding meeting the criteria in Article 107(1) of the Treaty constitutes State aid and requires notification to the Commission by virtue of Article 108(3) of the Treaty. However, according to Article 109 of the Treaty, the Council may determine categories of aid that are exempted from this notification requirement. In accordance with Article 108(4) of the Treaty the Commission may adopt regulations relating to those categories of State aid.

Aid that fulfils all the conditions laid down in this Regulation both general and specific to the relevant categories of aid should be exempted from the notification obligation laid down in Article 108(3) of the Treaty.

This Regulation should apply to the processing and marketing of agricultural products, provided that certain conditions are met. For the purposes of this Regulation neither on-farm activities necessary for preparing a product for the first sale, nor the first sale by a primary producer to resellers or processors or any activity preparing a product for a first sale should be considered processing or marketing.

The Commission should ensure that authorised aid does not adversely affect trading conditions to an extent that is contrary to the common interest. Therefore, aid in favour of a beneficiary which is subject to an outstanding recovery order following a previous Commission decision declaring an aid illegal and incompatible with the internal market should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation, with the exception of aid schemes to make good the damage caused by certain natural disasters.

This Regulation shall not apply to: (a) aid schemes which do not explicitly exclude the payment of individual aid in favour of an undertaking which is subject to an outstanding recovery order following a previous Commission decision declaring an aid illegal and incompatible with the internal market, with the exception of aid schemes to make good the damage caused by certain natural disasters; (b) ad hoc aid in favour of an undertaking as referred to in point (a); (c) aid to undertakings in difficulty, with the exception of aid schemes to make good the damage caused by certain natural disasters

Aid with identifiable eligible costs exempted by this Regulation may be cumulated with: (a) any other State aid, as long as those measures concern different identifiable eligible costs, (b) any other State aid, in relation to the same eligible costs, partly or fully overlapping, only if such cumulation does not result in exceeding the highest aid intensity or aid amount applicable to this aid under this Regulation.

Aid without identifiable eligible costs exempted under Articles 21, 22 and 23 of this Regulation may be cumulated with any other State aid with identifiable eligible costs. Aid without identifiable eligible costs may be cumulated with any other State aid without identifiable eligible costs, up to the highest relevant total financing threshold fixed in the specific circumstances of each case by this or another block exemption regulation or decision adopted by the Commission.
Operating aid may be granted for the operation of innovation clusters. It shall not exceed 10 years.
The aid intensity of operating aid shall not exceed 50 % of the total eligible costs during the period over which the aid is granted.

Any concession or other entrustment to a third party to construct, upgrade and/or operate the sport or multifunctional recreational infrastructure shall be assigned on a open, transparent and non-discriminatory basis, having due regard to the applicable procurement rules.

For investment aid for sport and multifunctional recreational infrastructure, the aid amount shall not exceed the difference between the eligible costs and the operating profit of the investment. The operating profit shall be deducted from the eligible costs ex ante, on the basis of reasonable projections, or through a claw-back mechanism.

For operating aid for sport infrastructure, the aid amount shall not exceed the operating losses over the relevant period. This shall be ensured ex ante, on the basis of reasonable projections, or through a claw-back mechanism.

European Court of Human Rights established by this Convention,
Have agreed as follows:
ARTICLE 1
Obligation to respect Human Rights
The High Contracting Parties shall secure to everyone within their
jurisdiction the rights and freedoms defined in Section I of this
Convention.
SECTION I
RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS
ARTICLE 2
Right to life
1. Everyone’s right to life shall be protected by law. No one
shall be deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of
a sentence of a court following his conviction of a crime for which
this penalty is provided by law.
2. Deprivation of life shall not be regarded as inflicted in
contravention of this Article when it results from the use of force
which is no more than absolutely necessary:
(a) in defence of any person from unlawful violence;
(b) in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape
of a person lawfully detained;
(c) in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot
or insurrection.
ARTICLE 3
Prohibition of torture
No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading
treatment or punishment.
ARTICLE 4
Prohibition of slavery and forced labour
1. No one shall be held in slavery or servitude.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER TO THE TWO QUESTIONS

1. MAY A CONTRACTING STATE DEROGATE FROM ARTICLE 3 UNDER THE ARTICLE 15 EMERGENCY PROVISION DURING A WAR? — NO.

Article 15(1) ECHR opens the door: 'In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law.' That general power is then closed, right-of-way, by Article 15(2):

   'No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision.'

Article 3 (prohibition of torture and of inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment) is named in that list. The consequence is categorical: there is no state of war, no public emergency, no level of exigency, and no notification under Article 15(3) that can authorise a derogation from Article 3. The prohibition is non-derogable as a matter of the treaty text itself, not merely as a matter of judicial interpretation. The European Court of Human Rights' own Guide on Article 15 states the point in terms: 'Article 15 § 2 protects certain fundamental rights in the Convention from any derogation' (§ 38), the protected rights being 'Article 2 (the right to life), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war; Article 3 (the prohibition of torture and other forms of ill-treatment); Article 4 § 1 (the prohibition of slavery or servitude); and Article 7 (no punishment without law)', and 'The effect of Article 15 § 2 ... is that the rights to which they refer continue to apply during any time of war or public emergency, irrespective of any derogation made by a Contracting State' (§ 40).

Corollary points a State's legal adviser should record:
- A derogation notice that purports to cover Article 3 is ineffective as to Article 3. It does not become effective by being notified to the Secretary General under Article 15(3); notification is a procedural condition of a valid derogation, not a source of power to derogate from a non-derogable right.
- Article 15(1)'s two independent gates — 'strictly required by the exigencies of the situation' and 'not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law' — continue to apply to any measures actually taken. Even for derogable rights, the margin is supervised by the Court.
- A reservation under Article 57 cannot be used to achieve what Article 15(2) forbids; reservations of general character are not permitted, and a reservation against Article 3 would be incompatible with the object and purpose of the Convention.
- Denunciation under Article 58 does not retroactively release a State from responsibility for acts committed while a Party.
- Article 17 (prohibition of abuse of rights) prevents Article 15 from being read as a licence to destroy Convention rights.

2. WHAT NARROW ARTICLE 2 EXCEPTION DOES THE SAME NON-DEROGATION CLAUSE STATE? — DEATHS RESULTING FROM LAWFUL ACTS OF WAR.

The exception sits inside Article 15(2) itself, as a carve-out attached to Article 2 only: 'No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, ...'. The ECtHR Guide describes it as an addition: 'Article 15 § 2 adds the additional exception that the right to life will not be violated if the death results from a lawful act of war' (§ 42).

Three limits on the exception must be stated precisely, because it is narrow:
(a) Subject-matter limit — it applies to Article 2 and to nothing else. It creates no licence regarding Article 3, 4(1) or 7.
(b) Qualitative limit — the death must result from a *lawful* act of war. 'Lawful' is doing real work: the act must be lawful under the applicable law, including the State's obligations under international law, which Article 15(1) independently requires measures not to be inconsistent with. An unlawful killing in war (e.g. a killing that violates the laws of armed conflict) is not covered by the exception; it is not a 'lawful act of war' and it is not a 'death resulting from lawful acts of war'.
(c) Structural limit — it is not a free-standing licence to kill. It operates so that, where the conditions are met, the death is not treated as a violation of Article 2 notwithstanding the absence of a valid derogation.

DISTINCTION THE QUESTION INVITES: Article 15(2) exception vs Article 2(2) intrinsic exceptions
These are two different things and must not be conflated.
- Article 2(2)(a)–(c) contains exceptions intrinsic to the right itself: deprivation of life is not in contravention of Article 2 where it results from force no more than absolutely necessary (a) in defence of any person from unlawful violence; (b) to effect a lawful arrest or prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained; (c) in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection.
- Those intrinsic exceptions are unaffected by any emergency: the Guide is explicit that 'In respect of Articles 2 and 7 of the Convention, the exceptions already contained in those rights will also continue to apply' (§ 41), and that Article 15(2) 'adds the additional exception' of lawful acts of war (§ 42).
- So the correct analytical order is: (i) is the deprivation of life covered by Article 2(2)(a)–(c)? If yes, no violation, no derogation analysis needed. (ii) If not, is it a death resulting from a lawful act of war under Article 15(2)? If yes, no violation notwithstanding the absence of a valid derogation. (iii) If neither, Article 2 is violated, and no Article 15 derogation can cure it.

TABLE: NON-DEROGABLE RIGHTS UNDER ARTICLE 15(2) (as the text lists them)
| Right | Derogable under Art. 15? | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Art. 2 — right to life | No, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war | Intrinsic Art. 2(2)(a)–(c) exceptions also continue to apply |
| Art. 3 — prohibition of torture / inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment | No, absolutely | No exception of any kind is stated |
| Art. 4(1) — prohibition of slavery and servitude | No | Only paragraph 1; Art. 4(2)–(3) (forced labour) is not in the list |
| Art. 7 — no punishment without law | No | Art. 7(2) intrinsic exception continues to apply |
| All other Convention rights (e.g. Arts. 5, 6, 8–11, 14) | Yes, in principle | Subject to Art. 15(1): strictly required by the exigencies; not inconsistent with other international law obligations; Art. 15(3) notification |

PROTOCOL INTERACTION (from the same fetched Convention text)
- Protocol No. 6 Article 2 ('Death penalty in time of war') permits a State to make provision in its law for the death penalty in respect of acts committed in time of war or imminent threat of war, applied only in the instances laid down in law and in accordance with its provisions, with communication to the Secretary General. Protocol No. 6 Article 3 ('Prohibition of derogations') then states: 'No derogation from the provisions of this Protocol shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention.' Protocol No. 6 Article 4 bars reservations under Article 57.
- A further protocol contains the clause 'No derogation from this Article shall be made under Article15 of the Convention', and another bars reservations in respect of its provisions. The Guide confirms at § 39 that 'Three of the additional protocols to the Convention also contain clauses which prohibit derogation from certain of the rights contained in them' and that the effect of Article 15(2) and those corresponding clauses is that the rights 'continue to apply during any time of war or public emergency' (§ 40).
- Practical consequence: even where a Protocol permits a death penalty in time of war as a matter of the State's domestic law, that Protocol's own non-derogation clause prevents using Article 15 to expand it, and the Article 15(2) 'lawful acts of war' exception still governs whether a particular death is attributable to a lawful act of war.

OPERATIONAL CHECKLIST FOR A CONTRACTING STATE INVOKING ARTICLE 15 IN A WAR
1. Do not notify any derogation from Article 3, 4(1) or 7 — it is legally a nullity as to those rights and creates litigation risk and diplomatic cost.
2. Treat Article 2 as non-derogable except for deaths resulting from lawful acts of war; do not rely on Article 15 to authorise any killing that is not a lawful act of war.
3. Test every proposed measure against Article 15(1) twice: (i) strictly required by the exigencies of the situation (individualised, evidenced, time-limited, reviewable — the Court examines whether the State has 'gone beyond the "extent strictly required by the exigencies"'); (ii) not inconsistent with the State's other obligations under international law (the Court will consider this limb of its own motion).
4. Notify the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully under Article 15(3): measures taken and reasons; and notify when they cease to operate and the Convention is again fully executed.
5. Keep the derogation's scope ratione materiae and ratione temporis explicit; the Court may raise scope of its own motion.
6. Do not attempt to reach the same result by reservation (Art. 57), general character reservations being impermissible, or by denunciation (Art. 58), which does not release the State from responsibility for prior acts.
7. Apply Article 14 non-discrimination and Article 17 abuse-of-rights safeguards to the emergency measures.

PROVENANCE NOTE
Everything above is drawn from the fetched Convention text (Articles 2, 3, 4(1), 7, 15(1)–(3), 17, 57, 58; Protocol 6 Arts. 2–4; the further protocol non-derogation and no-reservation clauses) and the ECtHR Guide on Article 15 (§§ 38–42). One point is NOT in the fetched pages and is offered only as a cross-check to be independently verified before reliance: the UN Convention against Torture contains no wartime or emergency exception, which reinforces (but is not needed for) the conclusion on Article 3.

ON THE PROOF-OF-ABSENCE ENTRIES
The harness's absence searches used paraphrase strings ('absolute prohibition of torture', 'non-derogable right under Art 3', 'Article 2 exception for the death penalty', 'capital punishment exception', 'narrow exception to the right to life'). The Convention does not use those formulations. It uses the operative wording quoted above — 'No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision' — which appears verbatim in each Convention fetch and again in the Guide. The answer is therefore stated on the page, not absent from it, and neither ask belongs in not_stated.

UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006
UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006
The Model Law is designed to assist States in reforming and modernizing their laws on arbitral procedure so as to take into account the particular features and needs of international commercial arbitration. It covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award. It reflects worldwide consensus on key aspects of international arbitration practice having been accepted by States of all regions and the different legal or economic systems of the world.

Amendments to articles 1 (2), 7, and 35 (2), a new chapter IV A to replace article 17 and a new article 2 A were adopted by UNCITRAL on 7 July 2006. The revised version of article 7 is intended to modernise the form required of an arbitration agreement to better conform with international contract practices. The newly introduced chapter IV A establishes a more comprehensive legal regime dealing with interim measures in support of arbitration. As of 2006, the standard version of the Model Law is the amended version. The original 1985 text is also reproduced in view of the many national enactments based on this original version.

UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules
The UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules provide a comprehensive set of procedural rules upon which parties may agree for the conduct of arbitral proceedings arising out of their commercial relationship and are widely used in ad hoc arbitrations as well as administered arbitrations. The Rules cover all aspects of the arbitral process, providing a model arbitration clause, setting out procedural rules regarding the appointment of arbitrators and the conduct of arbitral proceedings, and establishing rules in relation to the form, effect and interpretation of the award. At present, there exist three different versions of the Arbitration Rules: (i) the 1976 version; (ii) the 2010 revised version; and (iii) the 2013 version which incorporates the UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency for Treaty-based Investor-State Arbitration and (iv) the 2021 version which incorporates the UNCITRAL Expedited Arbitration Rules.

quotes.text: The UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (as revised in 2010) have been effective since 15 August 2010. They include provisions dealing with, amongst others, multiple-party arbitration and joinder, liability, and a procedure to object to experts appointed by the arbitral tribunal. A number of innovative features contained in the Rules aim to enhance procedural efficiency, including revised procedures for the replacement of an arbitrator, the requirement for reasonableness of costs, and a review mechanism regarding the costs of arbitration. They also include more detailed provisions on interim measures.

International Commercial Arbitration
The Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York, 1958), better known as the New York Convention, is one of the most important United Nations treaties in the area of international trade law and the cornerstone of the international arbitration system. Under the New York Convention, States undertake to give effect to an agreement to arbitrate, and to recognize and enforce awards made in other States. In 2006, a Recommendation regarding the interpretation of articles II(2) and VII(1) was adopted and in 2016, the UNCITRAL Secretariat Guide on the New York Convention was published.

verdict.summary:
# Retrieval instruction: which UNCITRAL text to retrieve

## 1. Answer

Retrieve the **UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006** — commonly cited as the "UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration" or "Model Law".

- Landing page / retrieval point: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration
- Retrieve the document listed there as *"Text of the Model Law (amended in 2006) - Explanatory Note"* (the amended text plus the Explanatory Note), and take the General Assembly resolution 61/33 (2006) as the adoption authority for the amended version.
- Do **not** retrieve the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules for this purpose (see section 4).

## 2. Why this text and not another — the mapping is verbatim

The UNCITRAL page for the Model Law describes the instrument in terms that map one-to-one onto the four topics the team listed:

> "It covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award."
> — https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration (fetched 2026-11-22T23:53:58Z, sha256 2b767ee0758e)

| Team's stated topic | Wording on the Model Law page |
|---|---|
| The arbitration agreement | "the arbitration agreement" |
| Tribunal composition and jurisdiction | "the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal" |
| Court intervention | "the extent of court intervention" |
| Recognition and enforcement of the award | "the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award" |

All four listed topics are covered, and the page frames the instrument as the one designed to "assist States in reforming and modernizing their laws on arbitral procedure" — i.e. it is the legislative/model text, not a set of procedural rules.

## 3. Which version to retrieve (this matters for two of the four topics)

The page states: **"As of 2006, the standard version of the Model Law is the amended version."** The 2006 amendments were to articles 1(2), 7 and 35(2), plus a new chapter IV A replacing article 17 and a new article 2 A, adopted 7 July 2006.

Two of those amendments land directly on the team's topics, so the amended text is the correct default:

- **Article 7 (arbitration agreement)** — "The revised version of article 7 is intended to modernise the form required of an arbitration agreement to better conform with international contract practices." Relevant to the team's first topic and to whether a cross-border clause will satisfy a writing/form requirement.
- **Article 35(2) and new chapter IV A (interim measures)** — "The newly introduced chapter IV A establishes a more comprehensive legal regime dealing with interim measures in support of arbitration." Relevant to enforcement and to court-ordered interim relief.

Retrieve the **original 1985 text only as a secondary document**, and only for the purpose of checking a State that enacted the pre-2006 version: the page notes "The original 1985 text is also reproduced in view of the many national enactments based on this original version." If the team's jurisdictions enacted the 1985 text, articles 7 and 17 in their law will not read as the amended text does.

## 4. What not to retrieve, and why (negative confirmation)

The plausible alternative is the **UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules** (1976; revised 2010; 2013 version incorporating the Rules on Transparency; 2021 version incorporating the Expedited Arbitration Rules). They are the wrong instrument for this request:

- They are "a comprehensive set of procedural rules upon which parties may agree for the conduct of arbitral proceedings" — i.e. they govern how a particular arbitration is run, not the national law on arbitration, and they say nothing about the extent of court intervention or about recognition and enforcement of awards by courts.
- The Model Law's four topics are matters of the seat State's law and of the enforcing State's law; the Rules are a contractual procedural code. A team that retrieved the Rules would not obtain text on court intervention or enforcement.

Negative confirmation from the pages read in full (this supports, and does not contradict, the answer above): the full text of the Arbitration Rules page (12,741 characters, sha256 81f0ae56c81c), the full text of the Arbitration Rules PDF (26 pages, 38,713 characters, sha256 de4f091bac5d) and the full text of the Arbitration Rules travaux page (24,144 characters, sha256 fa690d1e7442) contain **no occurrence** of "UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration", "Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration", "UNCITRAL Model Law" or "MLICA". The Model Law text therefore is not obtainable from the Arbitration Rules corpus at all; it must be retrieved from the Model Law page at the URL in section 1. (This is a proof of absence on those three pages only — it is not a statement that UNCITRAL's pages are silent on the question. The Model Law page answers it expressly, as quoted in section 2.)

## 5. Article map to verify against the retrieved PDF

The following is the structure of the amended Model Law, given so the team can check the retrieved text covers all four topics on arrival. **Verify each article number against the retrieved PDF**; the numbers below are the instrument's structure, not quotations from the fetched pages.

- **Chapter I — General provisions (arts 1–6).** Includes art 1 (scope of application), art 2 (definitions and rules of interpretation), art 2 A (international origin and general principles), art 5 (**extent of court intervention** — the provision that confines court intervention to what the Law provides) and art 6 (court or other authority for certain functions of arbitration assistance and supervision).
- **Chapter II — Arbitration agreement (arts 7–9).** Art 7 (**definition and form of arbitration agreement**; Option I and Option II), art 8 (**power of court to refer parties to arbitration** where there is an agreement), art 9 (arbitration agreement and interim measures by court).
- **Chapter III — Composition of arbitral tribunal (arts 10–15).** Art 10 (number of arbitrators), art 11 (**appointment of arbitrators**, including appointment by the court), art 12 (grounds for challenge), art 13 (challenge procedure), art 14 (failure or impossibility to act), art 15 (termination of mandate and substitution of arbitrator).
- **Chapter IV — Jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal (art 16).** Competence of the tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, separability of the arbitration clause, and the timing of pleas as to jurisdiction; art 16(3) provides for court review.
- **Chapter IV A — Interim measures and preliminary orders (art 17, with arts 17 A–17 J).** Added in 2006; the recognition and enforcement of interim measures is dealt with within this chapter (arts 17 H–17 I). Relevant if interim relief is in scope — flag to the team that this chapter exists only in the amended version.
- **Chapter V — Conduct of arbitral proceedings (art 18).** Equal treatment of parties.
- **Chapter VI — Making of award and termination of proceedings (arts 19–27).** Includes art 27 (**court assistance in taking evidence**) — a further court-intervention point.
- **Chapter VII — Recourse against award (art 34).** Application for **setting aside** as the exclusive recourse.
- **Chapter VIII / IX — Recognition and enforcement of awards (arts 35–36).** Art 35 (recognition and enforcement; grounds are stated exhaustively by reference to art 36), art 36 (grounds for refusing recognition or enforcement).

## 6. Complementary material the team will also need (retrieve alongside, not instead)

1. **Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York, 1958)** — listed on the UNCITRAL arbitration page. The Model Law's arts 35–36 are drafted to operate alongside it, and for any enforcement State that is not a Model Law State the Convention, not the Model Law, is the operative instrument. The page notes the Secretariat Guide on the New York Convention (2016) and the 2006 Recommendation on the interpretation of arts II(2) and VII(1).
2. **Explanatory Note / Guide to Enactment** accompanying the amended text — necessary for anyone reading the Model Law as a legislative template, because it explains which provisions are mandatory and which the enacting State may vary.
3. **Status of the Model Law** (the "Status" link on the Model Law page) and the **CLOUT case law / 2012 Digest** — needed to check whether the relevant jurisdictions have enacted the Model Law and, critically, whether they enacted the 1985 or the 2006-amended version.

## 7. Legal caveats to put in front of the team

- **This is an identification and retrieval answer, not legal advice on adoption.** If the team's real objective is to *adopt or adapt* the text into domestic legislation, that is legislative drafting work and is outside what this retrieval resolves; the Explanatory Note and Guide to Enactment are the starting point for that separate exercise.
- **The Model Law is not self-executing and does not govern a contract.** It is a template for State law. For a cross-border contract the operative texts are the chosen arbitration rules (for example the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, which carry their own model arbitration clause) and, for enforcement, the New York Convention plus the law of the enforcing State.
- **Check enactment status and version per jurisdiction before relying on the article map.** Articles 7 and 17 in particular differ materially between the 1985 and amended texts; a jurisdiction that enacted the 1985 text will not have the chapter IV A interim-measures regime.
- **Scope assumption:** the four listed topics are treated as the complete scope, per the request. If interim measures, conciliation/mediation or investor-State transparency are also in scope, say so — interim measures are already inside the amended Model Law (chapter IV A), but conciliation would point to the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules / Model Law on International Commercial Conciliation, and treaty-based investor-State arbitration to the Rules on Transparency.

## 8. One-line instruction to the person retrieving

> Go to https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration and download "Text of the Model Law (amended in 2006) - Explanatory Note"; also download the original 1985 text for comparison and the New York Convention (1958) as complementary material. Do not download the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules for this purpose.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — MINIMUM CAPITAL RATIOS UNDER 12 CFR 217.10(a), BEFORE ANY BUFFER OR ADD-ON

Authority: 12 CFR 217.10(a)(1) (Regulation Q; Subpart B, "Capital Ratio Requirements and Buffers"). Verbatim text read from the reproduced page:

  "§ 217.10 Minimum capital requirements.
   (a) Minimum capital requirements.
   (1) A Board-regulated institution must maintain the following minimum capital ratios:
   (i) A common equity tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5 percent.
   (ii) A tier 1 capital ratio of 6 percent.
   (iii) A total capital ratio of 8 percent.
   (iv) A leverage ratio of 4 percent.
   (v) For advanced approaches Board-regulated institutions or, for Category III Board-regulated institutions, a supplementary leverage ratio of 3 percent."

1. FLAT MINIMUMS (pre-buffer)

| Ratio | Minimum | Denominator basis | Cite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Common equity tier 1 (CET1) | 4.5% | standardized total risk-weighted assets | 217.10(a)(1)(i); calc. method 217.10(b)(1) |
| Tier 1 | 6% | standardized total risk-weighted assets | 217.10(a)(1)(ii); 217.10(b)(2) |
| Total capital | 8% | standardized total risk-weighted assets | 217.10(a)(1)(iii); 217.10(b)(3) |
| Leverage | 4% | average total consolidated assets (non-risk-based) | 217.10(a)(1)(iv) |
| Supplementary leverage (SLR) | 3% | total leverage exposure — only advanced approaches institutions and Category III institutions | 217.10(a)(1)(v) |

These are the requirements stated in the regulation itself, computed with no capital conservation buffer, no stress capital buffer, no countercyclical capital buffer amount, no G-SIB surcharge, no leverage buffer and no supervisory add-on layered on top. That is exactly the "before any capital buffers or other add-ons" figure requested.

2. QUALIFIERS A COMPLIANCE REVIEW MUST RECORD ALONGSIDE THE NUMBERS

(a) Community bank framework deeming provision — 217.10(a)(2): "A qualifying community banking organization (as defined in § 217.12), that is subject to the community bank leverage ratio framework (as defined § 217.12), is considered to have met the minimum capital requirements in this paragraph (a) of this section." So a qualifying community banking organization that has elected the CBLR framework is deemed compliant with the four ratios above; it does not have to satisfy 4.5/6/8/4 simultaneously. The 4.5% CET1 figure therefore applies to a Board-regulated institution that has not made that election.

(b) SLR is a separate, conditional line, not a fifth universal minimum. It binds only advanced approaches Board-regulated institutions and Category III Board-regulated institutions. Do not report 3% as a general requirement for all Board-regulated institutions.

(c) Advanced approaches ratio mechanics — 217.10(d): once an advanced approaches institution has completed the parallel run and received Board notification under 217.121(d), its CET1, tier 1 and total capital ratios are each the LOWER of the standardized calculation and the advanced approaches calculation. The 4.5/6/8 minimums do not change; the denominator can, so the capital needed to hit 4.5% can be higher than the standardized-only calculation implies. Total capital under the advanced approaches is measured using "advanced-approaches-adjusted total capital" (217.10(d)(3)(ii), with the 217.20(d)(3) deduction and the 0.6%-of-credit-RWA cap on excess eligible credit reserves).

(d) Denominator definitions for the leverage ratio and the SLR are set out in 217.10(c)(4)-(5) and 217.10(d)(4) (and, for the SLR, the total leverage exposure definition in the rule). I did not have those paragraphs reproduced verbatim in the fetched passages, so I do not quote them; the 4% and 3% minimums above are quoted directly and are unaffected.

(e) Capital adequacy overlay — 217.10(e)(1): "Notwithstanding the minimum requirements in this part, a Board-regulated institution must maintain capital commensurate with the level and nature of all risks to which the Board-regulated institution is exposed." Satisfying 4.5/6/8/4 is necessary but not sufficient; a supervisory assessment can require more.

3. WHY THE "BEFORE BUFFERS" FRAMING MATTERS (compliance consequence)

Subpart B sets the buffers by reference to these same minimums — e.g., the standardized approach capital conservation buffer for institutions subject to 12 CFR 225.8 or 238.170 is the lowest of (i) the CET1 ratio minus the 217.10(a) CET1 minimum, (ii) the tier 1 ratio minus the tier 1 minimum, and (iii) the total capital ratio minus the total capital minimum; the countercyclical capital buffer amount ranges from 0% to 2.5% of risk-weighted assets; an institution without a stress capital buffer requirement yet in hand uses 2.5%. The 4.5/6/8 figures are the floor from which those buffers are measured and below which the distribution restrictions in Subpart B engage. Operating to exactly 4.5% CET1 is therefore compliant with 217.10(a) but will normally leave a zero buffer and trigger payout limitations; the practical, buffer-inclusive requirement is higher. This answer deliberately states only the pre-buffer statutory minimums as asked.

4. VERSION CONTROL / SOURCE RELIABILITY

The identical paragraph (a)(1) text and the identical 4.5 / 6 / 8 / 4 (and 3% SLR) figures appear in every reproduction fetched: eCFR current 12 CFR 217.10 and Subpart B pages (sha256 11713cd13188, ad468c827fcb), the GovInfo CFR 2026 title 12 vol. 2 PDF for §217.10 (sha256 e5f9e1966448), and the GovInfo CFR 2025 title 12 vol. 2 XML for §217.10 (sha256 c804b50067be). Because the numbers are unchanged across these versions, the open question of exactly which "cited page" the requester meant, and whether it reflects current law or a slightly older annual CFR edition, does not affect any figure reported here. If a pre-2014 or proposed version were intended, the ratios would differ (e.g., no CET1 minimum existed before the revised capital framework), so the requester should confirm the page date if historical text was intended; on the current and 2025/2026 annual editions, the answer is stable.

5. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE RECORD

Minimum common equity tier 1 capital ratio: 4.5 percent of standardized total risk-weighted assets. (Companion figures in the same paragraph: tier 1 capital 6 percent, total capital 8 percent, leverage ratio 4 percent; supplementary leverage ratio 3 percent for advanced approaches and Category III institutions only.) All measured before any capital conservation buffer, stress capital buffer, countercyclical capital buffer, G-SIB surcharge, leverage buffer or other add-on.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE RECORDKEEPING NOTE — 17 CFR § 240.0-2(c), business hours / direct-transmission window

1. ANSWER AS STATED IN THE TEXT

§ 240.0-2(c) 'Electronic filings' reads, verbatim:

  'Filings made by direct transmission may be submitted to the Commission each day, except Satordays, Sundays, and Federal holidays, from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., Eastern Standard Time or Eastern Daylight Saving Time, whichever is currently in effect.'

Therefore:
- Daily submission window (ask 1): 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., Eastern Standard Time or Eastern Daylight Saving Time, whichever is currently in effect — i.e., 06:00–22:00 local Washington, DC clock time, a 16-hour window.
- Excluded days (ask 2): Satordays, Sundays, and Federal holidays. On those days no direct-transmission submission may be made under (c).

2. SOURCE AND VERSION CONTROL

Text taken from two independent reproductions that are verbatim identical (sha256 match on the eCFR pair, f86928af7bf9):
- GovInfo, CFR-2025-title17-vol4, § 240.0-2 (edition date 2025-04-01): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title17-vol4/xhtml/CFR-2025-title17-vol4-sec240-0-2.html
- eCFR current, title 17, part 240, § 240.0-2: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/part-240/section-240.0-2
Amendatory authority confirming the same paragraph: SEC Rel. 33-11159, 88 FR 12209 (Feb. 27, 2023), item 10 ('Amend §240.0-2 by revising paragraph (c) ...'), which also states: 'Consequently, we are revising Rules 110(c), 0-2(c), and 0-5(c) to replace "8 a.m." with "6 a.m."'. The source note in the CFR reads '[58 FR 14682, Mar. 18, 1993, as amended at 65 FR 24801, Apr. 27, 2000; 68 FR 25799, May 13, 2003; 73 FR 973, Jan. 4, 2008; 88 FR 12209, Feb. 27, 2023]'. Because the 2025 CFR volume and eCFR current agree verbatim with the 2023 amendatory text, the 6 a.m. start is the current reading and no version conflict exists.

3. PARAGRAPH ATTRIBUTION CHECK (guards against mis-citing)

The same section contains three different windows; the deliverable reports only (c):
- (a) principal office open 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., except Satordays, Sundays, Federal holidays.
- (b) paper submissions 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., except Satordays, Sundays, federal holidays.
- (c) direct transmission 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., except Satordays, Sundays, Federal holidays.
Any answer giving 8 a.m. or 5:30 p.m. as the direct-transmission window would be a paragraph-attribution error; it is not made here.

4. SCOPE AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER (compliance caveats)

- This answers only what the regulation text says about the hours during which a direct transmission may be submitted. It does not address the separate 'deemed filed' cut-off rules (e.g., Reg. S-T Rule 13(a)(2) and the parallel provisions for Forms 3, 4, 5, and Schedule 14N, under which a submission made on or before 10:00 p.m. is deemed filed the same business day). Those are distinct provisions and should be cited separately if the requester's question is 'when is my filing deemed filed' rather than 'when may I transmit'.
- 'Federal holidays' is used in the text without enumeration; the regulation does not list them. No list is supplied here, because supplying one would be an addition to the text, not a reading of it.
- Time zone is fixed by the text itself ('whichever is currently in effect' in Washington, DC), so no conversion is needed; users outside Eastern Time must convert.
- The parallel provisions § 230.110(c), § 232.12(c), and § 260.0-5(c) carry the identical 6 a.m.–10 p.m. / Satordays, Sundays, Federal holidays language, so this window is cross-consistent across the Securitas Act, Securities Act, and Trust Indenture Act rule sets; no divergence to reconcile.

5. RECORDKEEPING CONCLUTION

Ask 1: 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET (whichever of EST/EDT is in effect). Ask 2: Satordays, Sundays, and Federal holidays. Both values are drawn verbatim from the cited page and are corroborated by the amendatory release; no ask is blocked.

quotes.whole:
Article 26
Obligation to report transactions
1.   Investment firms which execute transactions in financial instruments shall report complete and accurate details of such transactions to the competent authority as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day.
The competent authorities shall, in accordance with Article 85 of Directive 2014/65/EU, establish the necessary arrangements in order to ensure that the competent authority of the most relevant market in terms of liquidity for those financial instruments also receives that information.
The competent authorities shall make available to ESMA, upon request, any information reported in accordance with this Article.
2.   The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 shall apply to:
(a)
financial instruments which are admitted to trading or traded on a trading venue or for which a request for admission to trading has been made;
(b)
financial instruments where the underlying is a financial instrument traded on a trading venue; and
(c)
financial instruments where the underlying is an index or a basket composed of financial instruments traded on a trading venue

5.   The operator of a trading venue shall report details of transactions in financial instruments traded on its platform which are executed through its systems by a firm which is not subject to this Regulation in accordance with paragraphs 1 and 3.
6.   In reporting the designation to identify the clients as required under paragraphs 3 and 4, investment firms shall use a legal entity identifier established to identify clients that are legal persons.

7.   The reports shall be made to the competent authority either by the investment firm itself, an ARM acting on its behalf or by the trading venue through whose system the transaction was completed, in accordance with paragraphs 1, 3 and 9.
Investment firms shall have responsibility for the completeness, accuracy and timely submission of the reports which are submitted to the competent authority.

Article 22
Providing information for the purposes of transparency and other calculations
1. In order to carry out calculations for determining the requirements for the pre-trade and post-trade transparency and the trading obligation regimes imposed by Articles 3 to 11, Articles 14 to 21 and Article 32, which are applicable to financial instruments and for determining whether an investment firm is a systematic internaliser, competent authorities may require information from:
(a) trading venues;
(b) APAs; and
(c) CTPs.
2. Trading venues, APAs and CTPs shall store the necessary data for a sufficient period of time.
3. Competent authorities shall transmit to ESMA such information as ESMA requires to produce the reports referred to in Article 5(4), (5) and (6).
4. ESMA shall develop draft regulatory technical standards to specify the content and frequency of data requests and the formats and the timeframe in which trading venues, APAs and CTPs must respond to such requests in accordance with paragraph 1, the type of data that must be stored, and the minimum period of time for which trading venues, APAs and CTPs must store data in order to be able to respond to such requests in accordance with paragraph 2.
ESMA shall submit those draft regulatory technical standards to the Commission by 3 July 2015.
Power is delegated to the Commission to adopt the regulatory technical standards referred to in this paragraph in accordance with Articles 10 to 14 of Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010.

quotes.whole:
Article 25
Obligation to maintain records
1. Investment firms shall keep at the disposal of the competent authority, for five years, the relevant data relating to all orders and all transactions in financial instruments which they have carried out, whether on own account or on behalf of a client. In the case of transactions carried out on behalf of clients, the records shall contain all the information and details of the identity of the client, and the information required under Directive 2005/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council (27). ESMA may request access to that information in accordance with the procedure and under the conditions set out in Article 35 of Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010.
2. The operator of a trading venue shall keep at the disposal of the competent authority, for at least five years, the relevant data relating to all orders in financial instruments which are advertised through their systems. The records shall contain the relevant data that constitute the characteristics of the order, including those that link an order with the executed transaction(s) that stems from that order and the details of which shall be reported in accordance with Article 26(1) and (3). ESMA shall perform a facilitation and coordination role in relation to the access by competent authorities to information under this paragraph.
3. ESMA shall develop draft regulatory technical standards to specify the details of the relevant order data required to be maintained under paragraph 2 of this Article that is not referred to in Article 26.

Article 26Obligation to report transactions
1.Investment firms which execute transactions in financial instruments shall report complete and accurate details of such transactions to the competent authority as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day.
The competent authorities shall, in accordance with Article 85 of Directive 2014/65/EU, establish the necessary arrangements in order to ensure that the competent authority of the most relevant market in terms of liquidity for those financial instruments also receives that information.
The competent authorities shall make available to ESMA, upon request, any information reported in accordance with this Article.

quotes.whole:
Article 26
Obligation to report transactions
1.   Investment firms which execute transactions in financial instruments shall report complete and accurate details of such transactions to the competent authority as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day.
The competent authorities shall, in accordance with Article 85 of Directive 2014/65/EU, establish the necessary arrangements in order to ensure that the competent authority of the most relevant market in terms of liquidity for those financial instruments also receives that information.
The competent authorities shall make available to ESMA, upon request, any information reported in accordance with this Article.
2.   The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 shall apply to:
(a)
financial instruments which are admitted to trading or traded on a trading venue or for which a request for admission to trading has been made;
(b)
financial instruments where the underlying is a financial instrument traded on a trading venue; and
(c)
financial instruments where the underlying is an index or a basket composed of financial instruments traded on a trading venue

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under the original text of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 (MiFIR), adopted 15 May 2014, an investment firm must report complete and accurate details of an executed transaction to the competent authority AS QUICKLY AS POSSIBLE AND NO LATER THAN THE CLOSE OF THE FOLLOWING WORKING DAY. The fixed backstop is therefore the close of the working day following the day of execution (T+1, by close of business).

PROVISION (verbatim)

Article 26 (Obligation to report transactions), paragraph 1, first subparagraph:

  'Investment firms which execute transactions in financial instruments shall report complete and accurate details of such transactions to the competent authority as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day.'

Citation: Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 May 2014 on markets in financial instruments and amending Regulation (EU) No 648/2012, OJ L 173, 12.6.2014, pp. 84–148, Article 26(1).

Source verification (all four renderings carry the identical operative sentence):
- EUR-Lex, original act, CELEX 32014R0600 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32014R0600 (sha256 deeb8d37c61c)
- EUR-Lex, consolidated text 17.01.2025, 02014R0600 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:02014R0600-20250117 (sha256 b72ebadf61ef)
- legislation.gov.uk, 'adopted' (as adopted) version of Article 26 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2014/600/article/26/adopted (sha256 3afbbd1054e3)
- legislation.gov.uk, revised version — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2014/600/article/26 (sha256 4f46d9f0944b)

SCOPE AND INTERPRETATION NOTES (compliance-relevant)

1. 'Working day', not 'trading day'. The adopted text of Article 26(1) uses 'working day'. It does not use 'trading day' and does not specify a clock time (e.g. 17:00 CET). Operational consequence: the deadline is the close of the next working day measured from the date of execution; the practical cut-off is set by the competent authority's reporting-system opening hours, and firms should confirm the national cut-off with their competent authority rather than assume a time-of-day in the Regulation.

2. 'As quickly as possible' is an independent obligation, not mere preamble. The Article is conjunctive: reporting as quickly as possible is required, and the close of the following working day is the outer limit. A firm that routinely reports at the T+1 deadline for transactions it could report same-day is not, on the face of the text, discharging the first limb.

3. No deferral regime. Article 26 contains no deferred-publication or delayed-reporting mechanism for transaction reports. The only relief in Article 26(1)/(7) route is that where the transaction has been reported to a trade repository under Article 9 of Regulation (EU) No 648/2012 which is approved as an ARM, and the report contains the details required by Article 26(1), (3) and (9) and is transmitted to the competent authority WITHIN THE TIME LIMIT SET IN PARAGRAPH 1, the investment firm's paragraph 1 obligation is deemed complied with.

4. Outsourcing does not discharge the firm. Article 26(7): reports may be made by the investment firm itself, by an ARM acting on its behalf, or by the trading venue through whose system the transaction was completed — but 'Investment firms shall have responsibility for the completeness, accuracy and timely submission of the reports which are submitted to the competent authority.' Compliance control implication: the T+1 obligation must be monitored at the firm even where an ARM submits.

5. Errors and omissions. Article 26(7) requires that, where there are errors or omissions in transaction reports, the ARM, investment firm or trading venue reporting the transaction 'shall correct the information and submit a corrected report to the competent authority'. The adopted text does not state a separate express deadline for the corrected report; the correction obligation should be treated as falling under the same 'as quickly as possible' discipline. (Flagged as an interpretation, not a quotation of a deadline.)

6. Order transmission. Article 26(4): a firm transmitting orders must include in the transmission all details specified in Article 26(1) and (3); alternatively it may report the transmitted order, if executed, as a transaction under paragraph 1, stating that the report pertains to a transmitted order. Either route must still meet the Article 26(1) timing.

7. Related but distinct obligation. Article 25(1) requires investment firms to keep at the disposal of the competent authority, for five years, the relevant data relating to all orders and all transactions carried out. This is a record-keeping retention period, not the reporting deadline; it is cited here only to prevent conflation of the two.

8. Application date. The Regulation entered into force on 2 July 2014 (OJ publication +20 days) and applied from 3 January 2018, per the dates of effect recorded on the EUR-Lex page for CELEX 32014R0600. The Article 26(1) wording itself was not altered by that application timing.

9. Version control. The question asks for the original text as adopted 15 May 2014. The wording of Article 26(1) is unchanged in the 17 January 2025 consolidated version (verified above), so the answer is stable across versions for this specific sentence. The surrounding paragraphs of Article 26 have been amended over time (for example, the second subparagraph of Article 26(1) was expanded in the consolidated version to list points (a)–(d) of additional competent authorities to receive the information, and Article 26(8) on branch reporting was recast), but none of those amendments touches the T+1 deadline.

WHAT THIS DELIVERABLE DOES NOT COVER / NOT VERIFIED FROM THE FETCHED TEXT

- The article number of the ARM timing requirement in Title IV ('An ARM shall have adequate policies and arrangements in place to report the information required under Article 26 as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the working day following the day upon which the transaction took place') was not confirmed from the fetched passages; the sentence is quoted from the consolidated text but its article/paragraph number must be checked against the OJ before external citation.
- Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/590 (RTS 22), made under Article 26(9), specifies content, format and terminology of transaction reports; any timing content in the RTS operates within, and does not extend, the Article 26(1) deadline. The current consolidated RTS text was not fetched and should be checked before reliance.
- National competent authority guidance, reporting-system cut-off times, and any post-Brexit UK divergence (the onshored version retains the same 'close of the following working day' wording in the fetched text, with FCA substituted for ESMA/FCA technical standards) are outside the scope of this answer.
- No figure other than 'close of the following working day' is asserted. In particular, no 5-business-day, 2-business-day or 17:00 CET deadline exists in Article 26(1); those formulations were checked and are absent from the fetched pages.
