None of these is 45 days; only § 814.42(a) is. Note also that the 45-day period governs the **filing/acceptance threshold determination only** — it is not the approval decision and it does not stop the separate 180-day review clock, which begins on the date of filing.

## Point-in-time verification (as in force on 2026-11-21)

- Text checked: 2026-11-23T00:38:17Z (eCFR "current" Part 814, sha256 7c4288803759; § 814.42 page, sha256 1c98fcec130a; eCFR subchapter-C Part 814, sha256 7c4288803759; GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol8 Part 814 PDF, sha256 bb5f25146fd9; GovInfo Subpart C XML, sha256 9982d07e7ca4; FDA PMA Review Process page, sha256 3b780da1bd0f).
- The latest amendment recorded against § 814.42 in any source is **87 FR 2045, January 13, 2022**. Nothing in the grounding evidences an amendment to § 814.42(a) taking effect between that date and 2026-11-21, and the CFR-2025 bound volume prints the 45-day text unchanged.
- Residual gap, stated plainly: the fetch is two days **after** the target date. The eCFR "current" text at 2026-11-23 and the CFR-2025 volume are therefore being used as the best available evidence of the text on 2026-11-21, supported by the amendment history ending in 2022. To close the gap definitively, run the eCFR point-in-time query — `https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2026-11-21/title-21/section-814.42` — and confirm the operative sentence still reads "Within 45 days" and that the authority note lists no amendment dated between 2022-01-13 and 2026-11-21.

## On the harness's proof of absence

The harness searched the full text of all six pages and found none of "15 days", "fifteen days", "15-day period", "15 days after receipt", "15 days after FDA receives a PMA". That result is correctly read as **excluding a 15-day figure** from Part 814 — it is not a statement that the pages are silent on the question. The same full texts contain the 45-day sentence, quoted above and repeated verbatim on the eCFR Part 814 page, the § 814.42 page, the GovInfo PDF, the GovInfo Subpart C XML, the eCFR subchapter page, and FDA's PMA Review Process page. Ask 1 is therefore answered, not not-stated, and it is not blocked.

## Assumptions and scope

1. Scope is an **original PMA**. PMA supplements, HDEs, 510(k)s and IDEs have their own timelines and are out of scope; the 30-day HDE figure in the table is a contrast only and must never be substituted for the PMA figure.
2. "Days" = calendar days, per the working-days contrast in § 814.42(d)(2).
3. "Receives" means the date FDA receives the submission; where FDA refuses to file and the applicant resubmits, § 814.42(d)(1) resets the reference date to the date FDA receives the resubmission, and where a refusal-to-file is reversed after an informal conference, the date of filing becomes the date of the decision to accept (§ 814.42(d)(2)). The 45-day notification duty in § 814.42(a) applies to the original receipt.
4. A statement of the answer should be re-verified against eCFR before being relied on for any date later than 2026-11-23, since the figure is asserted as of a point in time.

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.230 Accepting a De Novo request.




(a) The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.






(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.






(c) 




(1) FDA may refuse to accept a De Novo request if any of the following applies:




(i) The requester has an open or pending premarket submission or reclassification petition for the device;






(ii) The De Novo request is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or does not contain each of the items required under this part, or a justification for omission of any item;






(iii) The De Novo request is not formatted as required under § 860.210;






(iv) The De Novo request is for multiple devices and those devices are of more than one type; or






(v) The requester has not responded to, or has failed to provide a rationale for not responding to, deficiencies identified by FDA in previous submissions for the same device, including those submissions described in § 860.220(a)(3).








(2) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, FDA will notify the requester of the reasons for the refusal. The notice will identify the deficiencies in the De Novo request that prevent accepting and will include the De Novo request reference number.





(3) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. The additional information must include the De Novo request reference number of the original submission. If the De Novo request is subsequently accepted, the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information.

        § 860.230
        Accepting a De Novo request.
        
(a) The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.

        
(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.

        
(c)(1) FDA may refuse to accept a De Novo request if any of the following applies:

        
(i) The requester has an open or pending premarket submission or reclassification petition for the device;

        
(ii) The De Novo request is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or does not contain each of the items required under this part, or a justification for omission of any item;

        
(iii) The De Novo request is not formatted as required under § 860.210;

        
(iv) The De Novo request is for multiple devices and those devices are of more than one type; or

        
(v) The requester has not responded to, or has failed to provide a rationale for not responding to, deficiencies identified by FDA in previous submissions for the same device, including those submissions described in § 860.220(a)(3).

        
(2) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, FDA will notify the requester of the reasons for the refusal. The notice will identify the deficiencies in the De Novo request that prevent accepting and will include the De Novo request reference number.

        
(3) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 21 CFR Part 860 (Subpart D), version in force 2026-11-21

QUESTION: FDA receives a De Novo request that is accepted without any additional-information submission. What are the outside time limits (a) for FDA's acceptance notification and (b) for FDA's review and order granting or declining the request?

ANSWER
(a) Acceptance notification: 15 days after FDA receives the De Novo request.
(b) Review and granting/declining order: 120 days after FDA receives the De Novo request.
Both periods run from the same event — FDA's receipt of the request — so they run concurrently. The outside limit for the entire matter, measured from receipt, is 120 days. It is NOT 135 days; the 120-day clock does not start on the acceptance date.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

1.1 Acceptance notification — 21 CFR 860.230(a):
"The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted."

1.2 Deemed acceptance if the acceptance review is not completed — 21 CFR 860.230(b):
"If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA."
Two operative consequences: (i) 15 days is both the notification deadline and the outer bound of the acceptance review itself — if FDA does not finish within 15 days, acceptance is automatic and the notification obligation continues; (ii) the date of acceptance is back-dated to the date of receipt, which is why the 120-day clock and the 15-day clock share a single start date.

1.3 Review and order — 21 CFR 860.240(a):
"FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b)."
The 120-day clock has two possible triggers: receipt of the request, or receipt of additional information that results in acceptance. Because the stipulated facts exclude any additional-information submission (no refusal to accept, no supplemental submission), the operative trigger is receipt of the request itself.

2. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21
Identical text appears in (i) the eCFR "current" page for 21 CFR 860.230 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:40:24Z, sha256 4b51e14960fd), (ii) the eCFR "current" page for 21 CFR Part 860 carrying § 860.240(a) (sha256 fffe7e6cc6c5), (iii) the eCFR Subpart D page (sha256 836c1be841b1), (iv) the GovInfo XML of CFR-2025-title21-vol8 § 860.230 (sha256 7fe7db912fc0), and (v) the GovInfo PDF of CFR-2025-title21-vol8 Part 860 Subpart D (sha256 917b0d666508). The GovInfo 2025 print edition carries an effective date of 2025-04-01 and already contains both the 15-day and 120-day periods. The only editorial note on Part 860 in the fetched text is a nomenclature note (73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008; 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021), neither of which touches these periods. No amendment affecting § 860.230(a) or § 860.240(a) appears between the 2025-04-01 edition and the current eCFR snapshot, so the figures 15 and 120 govern on 2026-11-21.

3. DAY-COUNTING AND TRIGGER
- Trigger for both periods: the date FDA receives the De Novo request. § 860.230(b) fixes the acceptance date as the date of receipt; § 860.240(a) runs from "receipt."
- Unit: the regulation says "days" with no business-day qualifier. Treat as calendar days. Caveat: Part 860 does not itself state a counting convention; the calendar-day reading is the standard FDA convention for these periods and is an interpretation, not quoted text.
- Concurrency: day 15 (notification) and day 120 (order) are counted from the same day. Worked example — request received 2026-11-21: notification due no later than 2026-12-06; order due no later than 2027-03-21 (using the convention that the receipt date is day 0). If a requester instead counted 120 days from the acceptance date, it would wrongly produce a day-135 outside limit.

4. WHAT DOES NOT AFFECT THE ANSWER
- Submission method (electronic vs. paper): neither § 860.230 nor § 860.240 conditions the 15-day or 120-day period on submission format. The only format-linked rule is substantive (refusal to accept for failure to follow § 860.210 formatting), which is a ground for refusal, not a different clock.
- MDUFA performance goals: commitments in FDA's performance-goals letters are not regulatory outside limits. The outside limits are the two periods codified in Part 860 above.
- Additional-information tolling: the stipulated facts exclude it. For completeness, on the face of the text the only restart of the 120-day period is "additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted" (i.e., after a refusal to accept under § 860.230(c)). A mid-review request for additional information under § 860.240(b)(1) does not, by the terms of § 860.240(a), restart or extend the 120 days.
- The 30-day figure: the only 30-day period in Subpart D near this subject matter is in § 860.260(a)(2), which attaches to a step following issuance of an order granting a De Novo request ("If FDA grants a De Novo request, within 30 days after the issuance of an order granting the De Novo request..."). It is not an acceptance-notification deadline and must not be substituted for the 15-day period. This is the reconciliation of the harness's proof of absence: the search confirms § 860.230 contains no "30 days" string; § 860.230 does contain the affirmative 15-day text quoted at 1.1. The page therefore states an answer rather than stating none, and ask 1 is not listed as not stated.

5. RELATED DEADLINES IN THE SAME SUBPART (for scoping, not part of the answer)
- Withdrawal of the request ends the review: § 860.250(a) lists the events (failure to respond completely to an additional-information request within 180 days; failure to respond to refusal-to-accept deficiencies within 180 days; denial of facility inspection; written notice of withdrawal) and § 860.250(b) requires FDA to notify the requester of withdrawal. None of these is a time limit for FDA to act on an accepted request.

6. LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
- This answer is confined to 21 CFR Part 860 as fetched. The statutory counterpart in section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act was not among the fetched pages and is not quoted here; if a downstream user needs the statutory 120-day provision as a cross-check, that text must be pulled separately and compared. No conflict is expected, but it was not verified here.
- The calendar-day reading and the day-0 counting convention in the worked example are stated interpretations; a requester whose internal SOP counts differently should record its convention explicitly.

7. ONE-LINE HOLDING
Under 21 CFR 860.230(a) and 860.240(a) as in force on 2026-11-21, FDA must notify the requester of acceptance within 15 days after receipt, and must issue the granting or declining order within 120 days after receipt; both periods run from the same receipt date, so the outside limit for the decision measured from receipt is 120 days.

C.05.014
During the course of a clinical trial, the sponsor shall inform the Minister of any serious unexpected adverse drug reaction in respect of the drug that has occurred inside or outside Canada as follows:

quotes.whole: FDA advises sponsors, as described in greater detail in the final ICH E2A guideline (60 FR 11284 at 11285 and 11286), to submit in written IND safety reports as much information as possible on a case. In some instances, information for final description and evaluation of a case report may not be available within 15 calendar days. Nevertheless, initial reports should be submitted within this timeframe when the following minimum criteria are met: An identifiable patient; a suspected medicinal product; an identifiable reporter; and an adverse event or outcome that can be identified as serious and unexpected, and for which, in clinical investigation cases, there is a reasonable suspected causal relationship between the investigational product and the adverse event (i.e., the causal relationship cannot be ruled out).

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DEADLINE CALCULATION — ICH E2A SEVEN-DAY EXPEDITED REPORTING

1. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS
- The case is assumed to meet the E2A criteria for expedited reporting as a fatal or life-threatening, serious, unexpected adverse drug reaction (SUSAR).
- Day 0 is the date the sponsor first receives information sufficient to meet the minimum reporting criteria: an identifiable patient, a suspect medicinal product, an identifiable reporting source, and a serious unexpected event for which, in a clinical investigation, a causal relationship cannot be ruled out. Day 0 is not counted as day 1.
- The E2A default periods are calendar days, not business days. Weekends and holidays count unless a binding local rule provides otherwise.
- No local jurisdictional variation or waiver is assumed. Binding local law may shorten or otherwise modify the E2A default and must be checked separately; where it does, the local requirement controls.

2. GOVERNING E2A RULE
ICH E2A §III.A.1 provides: 'Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report should include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products.'

3. CALCULATION
- Initial notification outer limit: end of day 7 after day 0, i.e. 7 calendar days.
- Follow-up outer limit: 8 additional calendar days after the date of the initial notification.
- If the sponsor uses the full initial period and notifies on day 7, the follow-up report that is as complete as possible is due by the end of day 15 after day 0: 7 + 8 = 15 calendar days.
- If the sponsor notifies earlier on day n (n ≤ 7), the follow-up is due by the end of day n + 8, which is earlier than day 15. Day 15 is therefore the outer limit measured from day 0 only when the full 7-day initial period is used.
- The 8-day follow-up period is not measured from day 0. It is anchored to the initial notification date.

Deadline table:
Day 0 — sponsor first knowledge; clock starts; day 0 is not counted as day 1.
Day 7 — outer limit for initial notification to regulatory agencies (7 calendar days).
Day 15 — outer limit for the follow-up report that is as complete as possible, if the initial notification is made on day 7 (8 additional calendar days).

4. CONTENT OF THE FOLLOW-UP REPORT
'As complete as possible' means the follow-up should provide the fullest available case information and, as E2A specifically requires, an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products. In practice this includes the complete case narrative, patient details, suspect and concomitant product details, event details and outcomes, reporter details, dates, causality assessment, relevant medical history, and the sponsor's benefit-risk assessment. If the initial notification was submitted on minimum criteria, the follow-up should fill the remaining data fields to the extent available.

5. PROCEDURE AND EVIDENCE
- Record the day 0 date and time, the source of the information, the minimum criteria met, and who determined that the case qualified.
- Submit the initial notification as soon as possible and no later than day 7; record the submission date and time and any regulatory acknowledgement or receipt.
- Submit the follow-up as soon as possible and no later than day n + 8 after the initial notification, where n is the day of initial notification; if n = 7, the outer limit is day 15 from day 0.
- If no additional information exists, document that the follow-up report is the complete report or that no further information is available. Do not silently omit the deadline.
- Retain the day 0 evidence and submission records for inspection.

6. BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
- This answer applies to the E2A seven-day rule for fatal or life-threatening serious unexpected ADRs. Serious unexpected ADRs that are neither fatal nor life-threatening follow the separate E2A 15-calendar-day initial reporting rule and are outside this ask.
- The 7-day and 15-day figures are outer limits, not targets; E2A requires notification 'as soon as possible.'
- If a local authority imposes a shorter period, the shorter period controls. If a local authority has a working-day rollover provision, apply that local provision only where it is binding; do not assume it under the E2A default.

quotes.whole: The IND format set forth in § 312.23 should be followed routinely by sponsors in the interest of fostering an efficient review of applications. Sponsors are expected to exercise considerable discretion, however, regarding the content of information submitted in each section, depending upon the kind of drug being studied and the nature of the available information. Section 312.23 outlines the information needed for a commercially sponsored IND for a new molecular entity. A sponsor-investigator who uses, as a research tool, an investigational new drug that is already subject to a manufacturer's IND or marketing application should follow the same general format, but ordinarily may, if authorized by the manufacturer, refer to the manufacturer's IND or marketing application in providing the technical information supporting the proposed clinical investigation. A sponsor-investigator who uses an investigational drug not subject to a manufacturer's IND or marketing application is ordinarily required to submit all technical information supporting the IND, unless such information may be referenced from the scientific literature.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER: The next submission must carry serial number 018.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (supplied eCFR, 21 CFR 312.23(e), 'Numbering of IND submissions')
"Each submission relating to an IND is required to be numbered serially using a single, three-digit serial number. The initial IND is required to be numbered 000; each subsequent submission (e.g., amendment, report, or correspondence) is required to be numbered chronologically in sequence."
(Identical wording in ecfr.gov title-21 part-312 / § 312.23, govinfo CFR-2025-title21-vol5 § 312.23 PDF, and the CFR-2022 XML — sha256 247f94aced1a, c9fcf5cc6176, 6fe868becbda, 5b1f51ad2205 respectively.)

2. CALCULATION
- Base: the initial IND is numbered 000 (regulation fixes the origin at 000, not 0001).
- Each later submission increments by exactly one, chronologically, regardless of type (amendment, report, or correspondence are all expressly in scope of the same single sequence).
- 17 later submissions therefore occupy 001 through 017:

  | Position | Submission | Serial |
  |---|---|---|
  | 0 | Initial IND | 000 |
  | 1 | 1st later submission | 001 |
  | 2 | 2nd later submission | 002 |
  | … | … | … |
  | 16 | 16th later submission | 016 |
  | 17 | 17th later submission | 017 |
  | 18 | NEXT submission | 018 |

- General rule: serial = (number of submissions already made after the initial IND), zero-padded to three digits. Next serial = 17 + 1 = 18 → "018".
- Bound check: 018 is three digits and lies within the three-digit range 000–999; no rollover, no padding ambiguity.

3. RECONCILIATION WITH THE FORM FDA 1571 INSTRUCTIONS (flagged discrepancy, does not change the answer)
The Form FDA 1571 instruction pages (fda.gov/media/77596 and fda.gov/media/123543) state: initial IND = "Serial Number: 0000", next submission = "Serial Number: 0001", numbered consecutively thereafter. That is a four-digit rendering and is internally inconsistent with 312.23(e)'s "single, three-digit serial number." Under the form convention the 17 later submissions would run 0001–0017 and the next would be 0018 — four digits, i.e., not expressible as a three-digit number, which is precisely what the request asks for and what the regulation requires. The request directs the answer to the supplied eCFR text, so the regulation controls: 000 → 001…017 → 018. Recommend the sponsor's serial-number SOP follow 312.23(e) (000 base) and note the 1571 instruction text as a known FDA form inconsistency; do not let a CRO or eCTD tool default to the 0000 base.

4. CORRECTION TO THE PRIOR PROJECT ASSUMPTION
The project analysis assumed the initial IND is serial 0001 and the next submission is 0018. That base value is wrong under 312.23(e); the correct base is 000 and the correct next serial is 018.

5. SCOPE / CONDITIONS OF THE CONCLUSION
This holds because (a) all 17 intervening submissions were numbered serially in one chronological sequence as 312.23(e) requires (no gaps, no voids, no renumbering, no administrative cancellation), and (b) none of them was filed as a separate IND (a separate IND under 312.30 for exception-from-informed-consent emergency research would start its own 000 sequence). Before filing, confirm against FDA's acknowledgment/correspondence for the most recent submission that it was in fact serial 017; if the last acknowledged serial differs, the next serial is that serial plus one, still zero-padded to three digits.

6. ENTRY ON THE SUBMISSION
Form FDA 1571, Field 11 (SERIAL NUMBER): enter "018" (three digits, no prefix, no leading 'IND' in the field itself).

7. NOTE ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE
The harness established that the literal string "019" does not appear in the eCFR § 312.23 page or the four other fetched sources. That is an absence of a specific literal string, not an absence of the governing rule: § 312.23(e) is present in full and fixes the numbering convention, from which 018 follows by the arithmetic in §2. The answer is therefore derived from the page, not reported as unstated, and ask 1 is neither blocked nor listed as not stated.

quotes.text:
§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.




(a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.




(1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or






(2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
quotes.whole:
§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.




(a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Subpart E—Premarket Notification Procedures
§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.
(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:

quotes.whole:
§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

verdict.summary:
# Regulatory determination — custom device under FDCA § 520(b); 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E; as in force 2026-11-21

## 1. Question presented

A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

## 2. Answer

**No.** A device that is within the meaning of FDCA § 520(b) is exempt from the premarket notification requirements of 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, by operation of **21 CFR 807.85(a)**. The 90-day advance-submission obligation in **21 CFR 807.81(a)** therefore does not attach, and no 510(k) need be submitted before the device is introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

The exemption is from Subpart E premarket notification **only**. It is not a general exemption from FDA device regulation (see § 5 below).

## 3. Controlling text relied on

**21 CFR 807.81(a)** (the rule that would otherwise apply):

> “Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria: (1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II. (2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section. (3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use…”

**21 CFR 807.85** (the exemption):

> “§ 807.85 Exemption from premarket notification.
> (a) A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
> (1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); or
> (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
> (b) A distributor who places a device into commercial distribution for the first time under his own name and a repackager who places his own name on a device and does not change any other labeling or otherwise affect the device shall be exempted from the premarket notification requirements of this subpart if: (1) The device was in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976; or (2) A premarket notification submission was filed by another person.
> [42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]”

## 4. Analysis

1. **The general rule is conditional, and the condition fails here.** § 807.81(a) obliges a 90-day advance premarket notification only for a device meeting one of the criteria in (a)(1)–(3). § 807.85(a) removes a § 520(b) custom device from “the premarket notification requirements of this subpart” — i.e., from Subpart E as a whole, including § 807.81.
2. **The statutory carve-out is not in § 807.81(b).** The exceptions listed in § 807.81(b) are a pending PMA/reclassification petition and a cleared PCCP. The custom-device carve-out operates independently, through § 807.85, and is keyed expressly to § 520(b).
3. **The premise satisfies the only regulatory condition.** § 807.85(a) applies “if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b).” The question stipulates that it is. Paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) restate the two statutory prongs — named-patient order, or physician/dentist-only use not generally available to or generally used by others — so a device meeting § 520(b) necessarily satisfies one of them.
4. **Result.** No premarket notification submission, and therefore no 90-day pre-submission interval, is required for this device on the stipulated facts. Because no submission is required, the corollary rule in Subpart E that marketing may not begin “until the applicant receives an order declaring a device substantially equivalent” is likewise inapplicable.

## 5. What the exemption does not reach

§ 807.85 exempts from Subpart E premarket notification only. A manufacturer of a custom device remains subject to, at minimum:

| Requirement | Status | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Establishment registration and device listing | Applies | 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart B (§ 807.20 et seq.) |
| Quality system regulation | Applies | 21 CFR Part 820 |
| Medical Device Reporting | Applies | 21 CFR Part 803 |
| Labeling | Applies | 21 CFR Part 801 |
| Unique Device Identification | Applies | 21 CFR Part 830 |
| Corrections and removals | Applies | 21 CFR Part 806 |
| Adulteration / misbranding prohibitions | Applies | FDCA §§ 501, 502 |
| Investigational device requirements, if used investigational | Applies | 21 CFR Part 812 |
| Premarket notification (510(k)) | **Exempt** | 21 CFR 807.85(a) |

A manufacturer must also not represent that the device has “FDA approval” or is “510(k) cleared” — Subpart E states that any representation creating an impression of official approval because of compliance with the premarket notification regulations is misleading and constitutes misbranding (21 CFR 807.97).

## 6. Conditions the manufacturer must keep satisfying

The exemption is not self-executing and is not permanent. To rely on it for each unit distributed, the manufacturer should be able to document:

- **The qualifying basis** — either (i) a physician’s or dentist’s order naming the patient and the device, or (ii) that the device is intended solely for use by the ordering practitioner and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other practitioners.
- **The statutory conditions added by FDASIA (Pub. L. 112-144, § 617, 2012)**, which are statutory rather than codified in § 807.85 and are therefore not visible in the regulatory text quoted above. These include the volume limitation on the physician-use prong — commonly stated as no more than **5 units per year of a device type** — and the manufacturer reporting obligation for custom devices. *Action item: verify the current codified text of FDCA § 520(b)(2)–(3) before relying on the exemption for a distribution program, because the question’s stipulation (“meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b)”) assumes these are satisfied but does not prove it.*
- **Non-general availability.** If the device is catalogued, advertised, or sold to the general practitioner market, the (a)(2) basis is lost and the device is no longer within § 520(b).

**Kill trigger:** if any element above fails for a given device or year, the exemption in § 807.85(a) is unavailable, and the device falls back under § 807.81(a): a premarket notification must be submitted **at least 90 days before** commercial distribution.

## 7. Currency and as-of date

- Text verified against the eCFR “current” edition of 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E (including the section-level pages for §§ 807.81 and 807.85), retrieved **2026-11-23T00:45:56Z** — two days after the 2026-11-21 as-of date — and cross-checked against the 2025 annual CFR print (CFR-2025-title21-vol8, Part 807 Subpart E). Both sources carry identical § 807.85 text.
- The source note for § 807.85 shows no amendment after **81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016**. § 807.81 carries a 2024 amendment (**89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024**) adding the PCCP exception at (b)(1)(ii); that amendment does not touch § 807.85.
- Residual risk: the retrieval reflects the codified text current as of 2026-11-23. If a rule amending § 807.85 or § 520(b) took effect on or before 2026-11-21 but is not yet reflected in the codified text, this answer would change. Nothing in the retrieved text signals such a change.

## 8. Note on the recorded proof of absence for ask 1

The harness searched the full text of the § 807.85 page for the literal strings “510(k)”, “PMN”, “90 days”, “90-day submission”, “Section 807.92”, and “21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E”, and found none. That is an artifact of the search terms, not silence on the question. Section 807.85 answers the question in its own operative words — “A custom device is exempt from premarket notification requirements of this subpart” — which use neither “510(k)” nor “90 days”; the 90-day clock is in § 807.81(a), a different section of the same subpart, which was also retrieved and read in full and which is quoted verbatim in § 3 above. Accordingly ask 1 is answered (No) and is not listed as not stated.

## 9. Procedure the manufacturer should follow

1. Document the § 520(b) basis in writing for the specific device before first distribution: named-patient order (patient name, ordering practitioner, device specifications) **or** physician-only use with evidence the device is not generally available to or generally used by other practitioners.
2. Confirm the statutory conditions (volume limitation, custom-device reporting) are satisfied for the year of distribution; calendar the annual review.
3. Do **not** submit a 510(k), and do not state or imply FDA approval or clearance.
4. Complete establishment registration and device listing; maintain Part 820, Part 803, Part 830, Part 801, and Part 806 compliance.
5. Re-assess at every change of intended use, marketing method, or distribution volume. On any loss of the exemption, submit a premarket notification at least **90 days** before distribution and do not market until an order of substantial equivalence is received.
6. Retain the exemption-supporting records for the life of the distribution program and at least as long as the Part 820 record-retention periods require.

## 10. Limits of this determination

This answers the legal question on the stipulated fact that the device meets § 520(b). It does not verify that any particular device in fact qualifies, does not address state or foreign requirements, and does not constitute legal advice; a device-specific § 520(b) qualification review should precede reliance.

TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB blood tests (sometimes called IGRAs) measure the immune response in whole blood after it has been mixed with controls and with synthetic peptides that are designed to simulate TB antigens. The white blood cells in most people who have TB infection are sensitive to the test antigens and release interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). The tests measure the amount of the IFN-γ response.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved these two TB blood tests that are commercially available in the United States:
QuantiFERON®-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus)

quotes.whole:
3. TB blood tests or TB skin test
There are two tests that are used to determine if a person has been infected with TB bacteria:
TB blood test (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test [TST])
Selecting a test
Health care providers may consider the reasons and context for testing, test availability, and the overall cost effectiveness of testing when selecting a suitable test for TB infection.
Health care providers are encouraged to use TB blood tests to detect TB infection. TB blood tests are preferred for:
People who have received the BCG vaccine and
People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation.
TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.
Interpreting test results
A positive TB blood test result or TB skin test result usually means TB infection. More tests, such as a chest radiograph, are needed to rule out TB disease.

quotes.whole:
Most people can receive a TB skin test. TB skin tests are contraindicated only for people who have had a severe reaction (e.g. necrosis, blistering, anaphylactic shock, or ulcerations to a previous TB skin test). TB skin tests are not contraindicated for any other persons, including infants, children, pregnant women, or people with HIV.
TB skin tests should not be performed on people who have written documentation of a previous positive TB test result (TB blood test or TB skin test) or treatment for TB disease. Most people who have a positive TB test result will continue to have a positive test result. Additional TB skin tests will probably not contribute to medical care, regardless of the result.
Health care providers should take into account the following factors when considering the TB skin test for a patient:
Age
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.

quotes.whole:
Health care providers treating children who have been vaccinated with BCG should also know that tuberculin reactivity is likely during the first two years after BCG administration to the newborn.
Multiple BCG doses (as practiced in some countries) increases a person's sensitivity to the TB skin test and the duration of positive TB skin test results after BCG administration.
BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.
Boosted reactions and two-step testing
A boosted reaction can occur in previously infected, older adults whose sensitivity to tuberculin has decreased over time. It also can occur in persons of any age who have been vaccinated with BCG or infected with mycobacteria besides M. tuberculosis complex. When given a TB skin test years after infection, these persons may have little or no reaction, giving a negative skin test result. However, the TB skin test may stimulate the immune system, causing a boosted reaction with a positive result after subsequent tests. The TB blood test does not boost subsequent test results.

quotes.whole:
Children younger than five years of age
Infants, children, and adolescents exposed to adults in high-risk categories.
Testing for TB infection if the child has received the Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine
The BCG vaccine may cause a false-positive TB skin test reaction. There is no reliable way to distinguish a positive TB skin test reaction caused by BCG vaccination from a reaction caused by true TB infection. Interpretation of the TB skin test reaction is the same for people who have had BCG vaccination as it is for those who have not.
Health care providers should recommend the TB blood test if a child:
Is five years of age or older and
Has ever received the BCG vaccine (TB vaccine).
Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by the BCG vaccine.
Conducting a medical evaluation
Health care providers should conduct a medical evaluation for TB disease for all children who have:
A positive test result for TB infection (TB blood test or TB skin test),
Symptoms of TB disease, or
Exposure to a person with TB disease.
A medical evaluation for TB disease includes:
Medical history
Physical examination
Test for TB infection (TB blood test or TB skin test)
Chest x-ray

Clinical Overview of Tuberculosis Disease
At a glance
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis).
TB bacteria usually attack the lungs, but TB bacteria can attack any part of the body such as the kidney, spine, and brain.
If not treated properly, TB disease can be fatal.
Overview
Not everyone infected with TB bacteria becomes sick. As a result, two TB-related conditions exist: latent TB infection (also called inactive TB) and TB disease.
People with TB disease:
Have a large amount of active TB bacteria in their body
May spread TB bacteria to others
May feel sick, and may have symptoms such as a cough, fever, and/or weight loss
Usually have a positive TB blood test or TB skin test result indicating TB infection
May have abnormal chest radiographs
May have positive sputum smears and cultures

quotes.whole:
Inform the method of diagnosis
Reveal factors that may affect treatment if the patient is diagnosed with TB disease
3. Test for TB infection
There are two types of tests that are used to determine if a person has been infected with TB bacteria:
TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test [TST])
Selecting a test
Health care providers should use newer TB blood tests to detect latent TB infection. TB blood tests are preferred for people who have received the BCG vaccine and people who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation. TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
A negative test result does not rule out TB disease or latent TB infection
Some patients with TB disease may have a negative result from a TB blood test or TB skin test. If a patient has symptoms of TB disease, health care providers should not wait for TB blood test or TB skin test results before starting other diagnostic tests.

quotes.whole:
Most people can receive a TB skin test. TB skin tests are contraindicated only for people who have had a severe reaction (e.g. necrosis, blistering, anaphylactic shock, or ulcerations to a previous TB skin test). TB skin tests are not contraindicated for any other persons, including infants, children, pregnant women, or people with HIV.
TB skin tests should not be performed on people who have written documentation of a previous positive TB test result (TB blood test or TB skin test) or treatment for TB disease. Most people who have a positive TB test result will continue to have a positive test result. Additional TB skin tests will probably not contribute to medical care, regardless of the result.
Health care providers should take into account the following factors when considering the TB skin test for a patient:
Age
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.

quotes.whole:
Health care providers treating children who have been vaccinated with BCG should also know that tuberculin reactivity is likely during the first two years after BCG administration to the newborn.
Multiple BCG doses (as practiced in some countries) increases a person's sensitivity to the TB skin test and the duration of positive TB skin test results after BCG administration.
BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.
Boosted reactions and two-step testing
A boosted reaction can occur in previously infected, older adults whose sensitivity to tuberculin has decreased over time. It also can occur in persons of any age who have been vaccinated with BCG or infected with mycobacteria besides M. tuberculosis complex. When given a TB skin test years after infection, these persons may have little or no reaction, giving a negative skin test result. However, the TB skin test may stimulate the immune system, causing a boosted reaction with a positive result after subsequent tests. The TB blood test does not boost subsequent test results.

verdict.summary:
MEDICAL CONSULTANT ANSWER — Ask 2 (verdict)

VERDICT: No. The stated preference for TB blood tests (IGRAs) on the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page does NOT apply to a 4-year-old who received BCG, because the page's preference statement is expressly limited to people 5 years of age and older. The child meets the BCG condition but not the age condition; both are required.

1. GOVERNING TEXT ON THE NAMED PAGE
Page: 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' — https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/ (page date stamp: Apr. 17, 2025; snapshot fetched 2026-11-23T00:48Z, sha256 9095c1db7f3e).
Verbatim, from the section 'TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])':
  'Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.'
This is the page's own statement of the preference, and it is age-qualified on its face. 'People 5 years of age and older' excludes a 4-year-old. The preference therefore does not reach this child.

2. CORROBORATION WITHIN THE SAME CDC 'CLINICAL TESTING AND DIAGNOSIS' SECTION (context, not the governing sentence)
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/clinical-and-laboratory-diagnosis.html: 'Health care providers are encouraged to use TB blood tests to detect TB infection. TB blood tests are preferred for: People who have received the BCG vaccine and People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation.' — and, in the same passage: 'Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.' So even where the BCG indication is stated without an age qualifier, the same page supplies the age rule that displaces it for under-5s.
- https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html: 'Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.'
- Note a genuine tension in the source set, reported rather than smoothed over: the same TST page also says 'BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.' That sentence is not age-qualified and pulls the other way. It does not change the verdict for this child, because (a) the named page's preference sentence is age-qualified at 5 years, and (b) the section's age-specific rule for children younger than 5 recommends the TB skin test as the method and routes any IGRA use in younger children to clinician judgement/AAP guidance. A 4-year-old falls squarely under the age-specific rule.

3. APPLICATION TO THE FACTS
- Age: 4 years → younger than 5 → outside the stated preference's age range.
- BCG history: present → satisfies the second condition, but conditions are conjunctive ('people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG vaccine').
- Therefore: preference stated on the page = not applicable. This is a statement about the default CDC-preferred method, not a prohibition. The page nowhere says IGRA is contraindicated, unavailable, or inaccurate under age 5; it says TST is the recommended method for that age group and that some experts use blood tests in younger children, with AAP guidance available for consultation.
- BCG-specific handling on the page: 'The BCG vaccine may cause a false-positive TB skin test reaction. There is no reliable way to distinguish a positive TB skin test reaction caused by BCG vaccination from a reaction caused by true TB infection. Interpretation of the TB skin test reaction is the same for people who have had BCG vaccination as it is for those who have not.' (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html). Practical consequence: if TST is used in this BCG-vaccinated child, do not 'adjust' or discount the induration for BCG — read it by the standard criteria — and treat any positive result as requiring the full medical evaluation (history, physical, repeat test as indicated, chest radiograph, specimen collection as indicated).

4. WHAT APPLIES INSTEAD — CLINICAL PROCEDURE FOR THIS CHILD
Step 1. Default method for a 4-year-old per CDC: Mantoux tuberculin skin test, with reading and interpretation at 48–72 hours by a trained reader; schedule the return visit at the time of placement (the page notes one advantage of IGRA is that only one visit is required, which is exactly why the 'might be less likely to return for reading' indication exists — if this child's family is at high risk of not returning, that is a documented reason to discuss IGRA).
Step 2. If IGRA is being considered for this 4-year-old (e.g., high likelihood of missed TST reading, clinical concern about BCG-induced TST reactivity, or family preference), treat it as a clinician-discretion decision informed by AAP guidance, and document the rationale. Do not describe it to the family as 'the CDC-preferred test' for this child.
Step 3. Confirm the specific assay's FDA-approved age range and the performing laboratory's validated age range before ordering, since the CDC page does not address test-specific minimum ages. The page lists the two commercially available assays as QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) and T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot) and states that FDA has approved these two; it does not state an age limit for either.
Step 4. Regardless of test chosen: a negative result does not rule out infection or disease. Per the page set, children under 5 with a known exposure should receive window prophylaxis even with an initial negative test if fewer than 8–10 weeks have passed since last exposure (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html). If the child has symptoms of TB disease, do not wait for immunodiagnostic results before pursuing chest imaging and microbiologic evaluation.
Step 5. Revisit the question at age 5: once the child is 5 years of age or older and has received BCG, the named page's preference for TB blood tests applies directly.

5. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
- The answer is strictly about what the named page states; it is not a recommendation that this child receive or not receive any specific test. Test selection remains a clinical decision with the treating provider, informed by exposure history, likelihood of TST return, assay availability/cost, and AAP guidance where relevant.
- The page does not address BCG-vaccinated children as a separate category from BCG-vaccinated adults beyond the age qualifier, and it does not state an assay-specific minimum age.
- Provenance assumption, stated openly: the ask specifies the page 'available on 2026-11-21'; the retrieved snapshot is timestamped 2026-11-23T00:48Z. The page carries an 'Apr. 17, 2025' content date and no intervening revision is indicated, so the snapshot is treated as the version available on 2026-11-21. If a revision landed between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23, this verdict should be re-checked against the 2026-11-21 capture.

6. NOT-STATED DETERMINATION (recorded so reviewers can see the reasoning)
not_stated is empty. The harness proof of absence supplied for ask 2 concerns https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html (33,773 characters, sha256 171f6557d84e) and searched for 'IGRA (Interferon-gamma Release Assay)', 'TST (Tuberculin Skin Test)', 'BCG-vaccinated', 'preferred', and 'children >=2 years'. That is a different page from the one ask 2 names, and the searched strings are not the words in which this answer is printed. Moreover the named page affirmatively answers ask 2, so there is nothing to report as 'the page states none,' and nothing is blocked.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD: On the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page (Apr. 17, 2025 version, available 2026-11-21), the stated preference for TB blood tests is limited to 'people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine'; a 4-year-old BCG recipient is below that age threshold, so the preference does not apply — CDC's recommended method for children younger than 5 is the TB skin test, with IGRA in younger children left to expert/clinician judgement and AAP guidance.

Context
High blood pressure (hypertension) is one of the most important, treatable causes of premature morbidity and mortality in the world. It is a major risk factor for stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cognitive decline and premature death. In 2015, it was reported that high blood pressure affected more than 1 in 4 adults in England (31% of men; 26% of women) – around 13.5 million people – and contributed to 75,000 deaths. The clinical management of hypertension accounts for 12% of visits to primary care and up to £2.1 billion of healthcare expenditure. Managing the cardiovascular events caused by hypertension also consumes considerable resources.
The guideline covers adults (over 18 years) with suspected or diagnosed hypertension, including those with type 2 diabetes.

quotes.whole:
Since the publication of the 2011 NICE guideline on hypertension, new studies have been published in key areas of management; in particular, the optimal method and threshold for diagnosis of hypertension, managing blood pressure in lower risk populations and reducing blood pressure to lower targets in people with hypertension (including those with type 2 diabetes). The updated guideline makes new recommendations in these areas, based on the evidence, that aim to improve care and reduce variation in current practice.
Treating resistant hypertension (when more than 3 drugs are needed to treat hypertension) remains challenging. New data was also reviewed in this area and the recommendations updated.
There is uncertainty in current practice about which people with symptomatic very high blood pressure (accelerated hypertension) to refer for immediate assessment. The available evidence was reviewed and new recommendations made to provide guidance for primary care on when to refer.

verdict.summary:
# Guideline identification for the primary-care hypertension pathway

## 1. Answers (for direct use in the pathway header and citation block)

**Ask 1 — which NICE guideline covers the scope.**
NICE guideline **NG136**, *Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management*.
- Reference number: **NG136**
- Published: **28 August 2019**
- Last updated: **26 February 2026**
- ISBN: 978-1-4731-9329-1
- Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:49:27Z, sha256 592a154eb06d)

Scope match is explicit, not inferred. NG136's overview states verbatim:

> "This guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (high blood pressure) in people aged 18 and over, including people with type 2 diabetes."

The Context chapter repeats it: "The guideline covers adults (over 18 years) with suspected or diagnosed hypertension, including those with type 2 diabetes." The recommendations chapter adds: "The recommendations on measuring blood pressure and diagnosing hypertension in this guideline apply to all adults, including those with type 2 diabetes." So 'adults with type 2 diabetes' is inside NG136's scope, not a separate guideline the team must bolt on.

**Ask 2 — which earlier NICE hypertension guideline it says it updates and replaces.**
**CG127.**

NG136 states it verbatim on its overview page:

> "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127."

Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:49:27Z, sha256 592a154eb06d)

The NG136 PDF carries the same relationship in NICE's standard replacement wording:

> "This guideline replaces CG127."

Source: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adultsdiagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:49:27Z, sha256 5db7a507a8f9)

## 2. Secondary replacement statement — record it, but it is not the answer to ask 2

NG136 also carves out the hypertension section of the type 2 diabetes guideline. Same overview page, immediately after the CG127 sentence:

> "It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28)."

The PDF words this as "This guideline partially replaces NG28." NG28's own page now points the other way: "For recommendations on hypertension in people with type 2 diabetes, see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults."

Use this in the pathway as a **cross-reference**, not as the predecessor: NG28 is the type 2 diabetes guideline, not the earlier hypertension guideline, and the replacement is partial (blood-pressure management section only). The earlier hypertension guideline that ask 2 asks for is CG127.

## 3. Why ask 2 is answered rather than recorded as 'not stated'

The absence proofs supplied cover four pages only — the NG136 recommendations chapter (sha256 1d1dd20857bd), the Context chapter (sha256 3776587fcf46), the Update-information chapter (sha256 e8839b7f6a90) and NG28 (sha256 81e1302ee0e1). None of those is the page that carries the replacement statement, and indeed the Context chapter refers to the predecessor only obliquely as "the 2011 NICE guideline on hypertension" without printing the reference.

The statement itself sits on the NG136 overview page and in the NG136 PDF, both of which were read in full and both of which print "CG127" explicitly. The condition for 'not stated' (the page states none) therefore does not hold, so nothing is recorded as not stated and nothing is blocked. Ask 2 is answered: **CG127**.

## 4. Currency and version control for the pathway

- Cite NG136 as last updated **26 February 2026**; the February 2026 change added recommendation 1.2.11 (healthy-living advice for people with raised blood pressure but no hypertension diagnosis).
- NG136's Update-information chapter also logs a **October 2026** amendment to recommendation 1.4.26 (hypertension with chronic kidney disease — when to use NG136 versus the CKD guideline), a **November 2023** postural-hypotension update (1.1.5, 1.1.6, 1.4.16 amended; 1.1.7 and 1.1.8 added; two blood-pressure-target tables added), and a **March 2022** blood-pressure-target recommendation for people with cardiovascular disease (1.4.23).
- NG136 is under active surveillance on antihypertensive drug response by ethnic group; NICE states it will check the evidence when published and decide whether to update. Flag this in the pathway's review log rather than assuming the drug-choice steps are frozen.
- NG28 is itself in update (atherosclerotic CVD, early-onset type 2 diabetes, obesity). Because NG28's hypertension section is already replaced by NG136, an NG28 update does not reopen the hypertension drug-choice steps — but the pathway owner should confirm this at each NG28 reissue.
- Confirm the full title of CG127 ("Hypertension: clinical management of primary hypertension in adults", 2011) against the CG127 page before printing it in the pathway. The fetched pages print only the reference "NICE guideline CG127"; the identifier is what the grounding supports and is what the answer rests on.

## 5. Points where NG136 and the type 2 diabetes population intersect (for the pathway build)

These are the places the team must not double-source from NG28:
- **1.2.12** — measure blood pressure at least annually in an adult with type 2 diabetes without diagnosed hypertension or renal disease; offer and reinforce preventive lifestyle advice. [2009]
- **1.4.24** — annual review of care for adults with hypertension (blood pressure, support, lifestyle, symptoms, medication). [2004]

§ 50.20 General requirements for informed consent.


Except as provided in §§ 50.22, 50.23, and 50.24, no investigator may involve a human being as a subject in research covered by these regulations unless the investigator has obtained the legally effective informed consent of the subject or the subject's legally authorized representative.
